#7226. Earth’s early crust left a fingerprint in rocks for a billion years, then it vanished

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (969 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Earth’s early crust left a fingerprint in rocks for a billion years, then it vanished

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lead in ancient rocks may help pinpoint when modern plate tectonics took hold and began reshaping how Earth recycles its crust.
  • Earth’s surface is made of plates that slide, collide, and sink back into the planet, and it’s tempting to assume it has always worked that way.
  • The signature comes from a pool of crust that formed roughly 4 billion years ago and kept getting remelted in place for more than a billion years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lead in ancient rocks may help pinpoint when modern plate tectonics took hold and began reshaping how Earth recycles its crust.

Earth’s surface is made of plates that slide, collide, and sink back into the planet, and it’s tempting to assume it has always worked that way. Rocks older than about 2.6 billion years carry a chemical signature that notes otherwise.

The signature comes from a pool of crust that formed roughly 4 billion years ago and kept getting remelted in place for more than a billion years.

Between about 2.75 and 2.63 billion years ago, the pattern changes sharply. One source’s signature vanishes from the record, and the other turns up only rarely after that.

The researchers interpret the shift as a possible sign that modern plate tectonics was taking hold and reshaping how Earth recycled its crust.

The study is an interpretation of a global compilation of lead measurements, and the authors call their explanation a testable hypothesis rather than a settled fact.

Janne Liebmann of Curtin University in Perth, Australia, led the work with colleagues at Curtin’s School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and Queen’s University in Canada.

“New crust often forms by melting older rock, leaving behind a distinctive chemical fingerprint,” Liebmann noted.

According to recent reports, the fingerprint is carried by lead. Uranium and thorium decay into three different forms of lead at three different rates. So the mix of lead in a rock records how much uranium and thorium its source held, and for how long.

It has been revealed that some minerals, including feldspar and certain sulphides, take in lead as they crystallize but almost no uranium or thorium. Their lead mix is fixed at the moment they form, which makes them a record of the magma they grew from.

In a recent development, the team compiled published lead measurements on such minerals from rocks whose ages were known independently. They added eight fresh feldspar analyses from China, West Africa, and Finland.

After discarding samples whose lead had been disturbed, 1,235 remained, with ages from 3.8 billion years to the present.

Recent findings suggest that in rocks older than about 2.6 billion years, the lead points to two sources that split from the mantle between 4.0 and 3.7 billion years ago. One was rich in uranium relative to lead, the other poor.

Both show up in rocks from ancient continental cores around the world.

For those signatures to develop, the two sources had to stay chemically isolated for at least a billion years.

The authors’ explanation is a primitive crust split into an upper layer and a lower layer, each with its own uranium budget, that magmas kept tapping without destroying.

Most of the old rocks in the dataset are granites, which can form when existing crust melts. That fits the idea that early Earth repeatedly reworked its crust in place.

After about 2.6 billion years ago, the lead in fresh rocks clusters near the average for the whole planet. The spread in the inferred uranium budgets of their sources roughly halves.

A statistical test for abrupt changes, repeated 300 times on reshuffled versions of the data, kept finding the same break between 2.75 and 2.63 billion years ago.

Recent findings suggest that the break held in the full dataset and in two subsets the team checked separately. Australian samples make up 71% of the compilation, so the authors treated the 358 non-Australian samples as an independent test. The break appeared there too.

Industry observers note that the uranium-rich source never reappears. The uranium-poor one surfaces only four times afterward, in granites from Russia and Australia between 1.6 billion and 400 million years ago.

Liebmann’s team wrote that the old sources were either destroyed, most likely by being dragged back into the mantle, or cut off from the places where new crust was made.

Both fit a planet that had begun moving crust around and recycling it, with magma production shifting from the interiors of plates to their edges.

Recent findings suggest that other changes geologists have documented in rocks of that age line up with the break. Continents were becoming thicker and richer in silica. Buried rocks began recording sharper contrasts in temperature. And what may have been the first supercontinent was assembling.

“It marks the transition from an early Earth where ancient crust could be repeatedly melted and reworked in place, to a system capable of moving and recycling crust on a much larger scale,” said co-author Chris Kirkland of Curtin.

Kirkland mentioned the finding helps explain when Earth developed the global system of moving plates that distinguishes it from Venus and Mars.

In a recent development, lead isotopes record that the old sources stopped feeding upcoming magma. They don’t by themselves show plates sinking.

The team wrote that direct evidence for global subduction at that time is limited, and that its model is a framework still to be tested.

The dataset also leans on Australia, where recent mapping projects have produced far more lead measurements than elsewhere.

The non-Australian check helps, but a more even global sample would test the result harder.

One detail may prove useful. The rare reappearances of the uranium-poor source suggest pieces of that ancient lower crust still survive under some continents.

According to recent reports, if so, they could account for part of a long-standing puzzle. Surface rocks on average hold more uranium-derived lead than the whole Earth should, which implies a hidden, uranium-poor reservoir somewhere below.

The team’s data are available through the EarthBank platform, where other researchers could test the break against fresh samples as they are measured.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society A.

#7225. China Just Sent a Robot to Harvest Rocks From the Pacific Abyss. Something Is Living Inside Them.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1132 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popularmechanics ↗ Open Full Page

China Just Sent a Robot to Harvest Rocks From the Pacific Abyss. Something Is Living Inside Them.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that somewhere in the eastern Pacific, between Hawaii and Mexico, a Chinese robot recently crawled across the ocean floor in total darkness.
  • The robot is called Kunpeng, after a legendary giant fish that turns into a bird.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that somewhere in the eastern Pacific, between Hawaii and Mexico, a Chinese robot recently crawled across the ocean floor in total darkness. The water around it was near freezing, and the pressure was immense. Over long stretches, it picked up loose rocks from the seabed one by one.

The robot is called Kunpeng, after a legendary giant fish that turns into a bird. It was built by the state-owned China Minmetals and used in what the South China Morning Post, citing Chinese state media, describes as China’s first large-scale deep-sea mining trial in international waters. Beijing hasn’t remarked much about the mission beyond that.

Industry observers note that what China was after looks unremarkable: lumpy, potato-sized rocks. But new research suggests these rocks hold something besides metal. Thousands of somethings, in fact.

They’re called polymetallic nodules, and they’re at the center of a deep-sea controversy that’s been building for years.

The problem has two parts. First, the nodules contain metals that modern technology depends on, including manganese, nickel, cobalt, copper, zinc, and iron. These metals go into everything from smartphones to electric vehicle batteries. Second, most of the nodules sit in the middle of the Pacific in a region called the Clarion–Clipperton Zone (CCZ), roughly 4,000 to 6,000 meters (about 2.5 to 3.7 miles) below the surface. Life in estuaries and tidal zones near the coast is used to constant change, from daily temperature swings to human interference. The deep ocean is far more fragile, however, so mining there could do far more damage.

Each nodule starts as a bit of ancient debris on the seafloor. Dissolved metals slowly build up around it in layers, adding only a few millimeters of rock every million years. One scientist told Popular Mechanics in 2024 that the process is “like a super slow game of Tetris.”.

According to recent reports, but as you might have guessed, there’s a catch. A latest study in the journal Scientific Reports found that the nodules aren’t just part of a delicate ecosystem. Each one is itself an ecosystem, home to dozens or even hundreds of tiny animals.

It has been revealed that the researchers analyzed 244 nodules and found more than 4,000 individual animals on their surfaces alone. The average nodule hosted 17 animals, but some held as many as 245 lifeforms, from single-celled species to nematodes and small crustaceans. The secret is the nodules’ porous structure: their crevices make ideal shelters.

“The crevices in the polymetallic nodules function as small shelters and provide home to animals that we do not encounter in the soft sediment of the seafloor,” mentioned Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo, a co-lead author of the study from the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research (NIOZ), in a press statement.

The surrounding mud held more life overall, but the nodules hosted their own distinct communities. Those communities looked alike from one nodule to the next and different from the ones in the mud. Some of the residents seem to live nowhere else. One species, a single-celled organism called Thurammina sp. 1, appears perfectly adapted to life on the nodules. If the nodules are mined, it could disappear along with an ecosystem that took millions of years to build.

It has been revealed that “Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules,” mentioned Sabine Gollner, the study’s senior author, who is also from NIOZ. “This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining.”.

In other words, the rocks China’s robot was gathering may be home to species that science hasn’t even named yet.

Kunpeng is built to survive in one of the harshest places on Earth. Researchers at Harbin Engineering University gave it a sound-based navigation system that can find its position to within a single meter, even in total darkness.

According to recent reports, to reach those extreme depths, however, the robot relied on specialized deployment gear. China lowered its submersibles 5,330 meters (17,500 feet) using the Haiwei GD11000, a deep-sea winch that Interesting Engineering notes is the only one in the world capable of reaching the ocean’s deepest point. While conventional research vessels use heavy, steel-wrapped cables that risk snapping under their own weight at extreme depths, the Haiwei system uses a 13-kilometer (8-mile) line armored with lightweight synthetic fiber. Over the course of the expedition, the winch completed six deployments—including a single 48-hour dive—logging nearly 200 hours underwater.

Recent findings suggest that the trial took place inside a 72,745-square-kilometer (28,000-square-mile) exploration block—an area larger than West Virginia. China Minmetals has studied the area since 2017 under a 15-year contract with the UN-backed International Seabed Authority (ISA). Beyond that, details are scarce.

According to recent reports, the stakes go well beyond science. China already dominates global refining of cobalt, nickel, and manganese. Mining the CCZ would let Beijing secure raw materials from international waters and protect its electric vehicle and battery industries from Western trade restrictions.

Industry observers note that and China isn’t the only country with its eye on these waters. Washington is moving to license commercial mining in the same part of the Pacific. While China works within the ISA system, the U.S. is using its own domestic laws, and it’s expected to rule by mid-December on a permit application from the U.S. subsidiary of The Metals Company, a Canadian ocean-mining firm.

It has been revealed that that name may sound familiar. The Metals Organization helped fund the 2024 research by scientists from the Scottish Association for Marine Science and Northwestern University that found possible evidence the nodules produce “dark oxygen,” a rare kind of oxygen production that doesn’t need sunlight. The company and other scientists have disputed those findings. The original team stands by its work and is now back in the CCZ studying the phenomenon.

No country has started full-scale commercial deep-sea mining yet. But China’s Haiwei winch is already set to join routine survey voyages, and a U.S. decision is weeks away. Meanwhile, scientists are warning that heavy machinery scraping the abyssal plain could permanently destroy ecosystems we’ve barely begun to study.

Sources indicate that dark oxygen or not, it’s increasingly clear that these nodules belong to an ecosystem far older than the first hominins, let alone Homo sapiens. Two superpowers are now racing to dig it up. Whether the creatures living inside the rocks will be named before they’re gone remains to be seen.

#7223. When AI runs the lab, who checks the results?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (910 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

When AI runs the lab, who checks the results?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A review across 11 fields examines how scientists test AI-generated results as machines take on more of the work of proposing and running experiments.
  • According to recent reports, it’s easy to picture AI in science as a very fast assistant: feed it the data and it finds the pattern.
  • Some AI systems now take on several steps in the research process, from reading papers and proposing hypotheses to directing robots in the lab and adjusting experiments based on the results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review across 11 fields examines how scientists test AI-generated results as machines take on more of the work of proposing and running experiments.

According to recent reports, it’s easy to picture AI in science as a very fast assistant: feed it the data and it finds the pattern. A review by researchers at 94 institutions calls that picture out of date.

Some AI systems now take on several steps in the research process, from reading papers and proposing hypotheses to directing robots in the lab and adjusting experiments based on the results.

The authors ask how much of what comes out of that loop can be trusted. They rank the field’s claims by how well each has been tested in the real world.

The review is a survey of published work across 11 fields, not a fresh experiment.

The lead authors include Yongjun Xu of the Institute of Computing Technology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Heyang Li of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Co-authors come from institutions including the University of Queensland and Berlin’s Hertie School.

Recent findings suggest that the authors’ own 2021 review, in the same journal, described AI as a powerful tool for analyzing data. AlphaFold, which predicts a protein’s shape from its sequence, was the model case.

That program answered one question that had resisted decades of work and left the rest of the job to people.

Five years on, the review describes systems built from six modules that feed each other.

One reads papers, one analyzes data, one proposes hypotheses, one runs experiments, one writes the report, and one adjusts the whole process based on what failed.

Large language models supply the knowledge and reasoning, software agents sequence the work, and robots supply the hands.

Some groups, the authors wrote, are already testing whether AI can take part in peer review itself.

In a recent development, the clearest example comes from materials science. An autonomous laboratory called A-Lab was handed 58 target compounds.

Drawing synthesis recipes from the literature and adjusting when a route failed, it made 41 of them in 17 days.

The review treats materials science as the field where the loop is most complete, with generative models proposing latest crystals and robotic platforms making and testing them.

Other fields are further behind. In medicine, the authors flagged limited prospective validation and the risk of fabricated outputs.

In geoscience, models trained on past conditions struggle when the conditions themselves shift.

Sources indicate that the review’s most practical contribution is a grading scheme. For each field, the authors coded the level of validation behind AI results on a scale from A to D.

According to recent reports, an A means a method has been experimentally validated or is already deployed in real workflows. A B means a prototype tested in a controlled, closed-loop setting.

A C means the result rests on benchmarks, simulations, or retrospective tests. A D means the work is still conceptual.

The point, the authors wrote, is that a high score on a benchmark is not the same as a discovery.

Closing what they call the reality gap between benchmark success and real-world use is, in their words, a top priority.

Industry observers note that three constraints recur across every field in the review. Standardized, high-quality data remain scarce.

Deep networks still trade interpretability for accuracy, so a model can predict a molecule’s behavior without explaining it.

And generative models can produce outputs that look plausible while violating physical laws, which the authors tie to the lack of explicit physical constraints in current architectures.

A fourth limit is human. The review cites earlier warnings that AI’s fluency can create what one group called “illusions of understanding,” with scientists mistaking output for insight and converging on the same few methods.

According to recent reports, the authors also put a price on scale. Global data centers used about 415 terawatt-hours of electricity during 2024.

The review projects that figure roughly doubling by 2030, an increase about equal to Japan’s current annual consumption.

For science, the authors wrote, the cost of discovery is becoming tied to electricity prices and hardware supply.

Recent findings suggest that in the United States, about 56% of data center electricity comes from fossil fuels. The authors put the resulting emissions at more than 105 million tons of carbon dioxide a year.

Training a single large model, they wrote, can cost from thousands to hundreds of millions of dollars, which risks a “computational divide” between well-funded labs and everyone else.

According to recent reports, A review maps what has been published, and the authors are candid that maturity is uneven and that the grades are theirs. The open question for any one field is the A-to-D test itself: has anyone checked the machine’s result against the world?

The authors expect the next decade to be the test. Governments in the United States, Britain, the European Union, and China have all debuted AI-for-science strategies.

The review’s case is that the advantage will go to whoever best combines data, computing, and people, not to the biggest budget.

Industry observers note that the authors’ closing line is a limit as much as a forecast. AI, they wrote, will serve as a cognitive copilot rather than a replacement for scientists.

The review was published in the journal The Innovation.

Tech Report: Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.
  • Sources indicate that some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Sources indicate that some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting firm in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

Recent findings suggest that the ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

It has been revealed that joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

Recent findings suggest that in the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

Industry observers note that the largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell indicates, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”.

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Firm. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, claims Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”.

Sources indicate that based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Firm was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

It has been revealed that beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data highlighted, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell notes, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”.

These fresh findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”.

Scientists Buried Sheep in a French Cemetery for a Year. What They Dug Up Could Change How We Bury Humans.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When someone dies and is buried, it’s often described as “returning to the Earth,” and strictly speaking, that’s true.
  • It has been revealed that this new approach to the afterlife is right now legal only in a dozen U.S.
  • According to recent reports, “It's the same principle as composting,” Charabidzé stated in a press release for the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When someone dies and is buried, it’s often described as “returning to the Earth,” and strictly speaking, that’s true. A body, typically pumped full of preservatives and chemicals in a traditional burial, is lowered into a perplexingly ornate casket, where it can take upwards of 15 years to fully decompose. However, a upcoming kind of burial known as “terramation” or “human composting” does away with these attempts at preserving the body. Instead, it leans into the opposite strategy by creating favorable microbial environments that can decompose human flesh in just a month. The result is a more eco-friendly end of life that doesn’t pollute the air like cremations, or leach chemicals into the ground as decomposing caskets do.

It has been revealed that this new approach to the afterlife is right now legal only in a dozen U.S. states, parts of Germany, and New South Wales in Australia. But France may be next, thanks in part to a strange experiment unfolding at a cemetery in Les Ulis. It’s here that Damien Charabidzé, an entomologist at the Université de Lille, is studying two types of burials side-by-side using sheep corpses. Last summer, Charabidzé teamed up with Humo Sapiens, a group campaigning to legalize terramation, to bury sheep in eight pits. Four sheep went straight into the soil, and four were packed in shredded plant matter.

According to recent reports, “It's the same principle as composting,” Charabidzé stated in a press release for the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS). “You need to strike a balance between a nitrogen-rich material to be broken down (in this case, a corpse) and carbon (wood shavings) through which oxygen can circulate.”.

Then the team waited a year and returned on a sweltering summer day to unearth their decomposed specimens. In the pits filled with plant material, no odors issued forth when the burials were exhumed. Only bones remained in the graves, with all organic material transformed into humus—stable soil organic matter. The same could not be stated of the other pits. There, the sheep had only lost only a quarter of their mass and many of them were in the process of saponification, in which fats from the body turn into a kind of wax (often referred to in human burials as “grave wax”).

“The flesh practically stops decomposing,” Charabidzé mentioned in a press release. “And nothing grows above the pit….We don’t know to what extent this natural phenomenon is exacerbated by embalming fluids, by the ingestion of food packed with preservatives during life, or by the deterioration of the soil in cemeteries.”.

Sources indicate that terramation solves several problems at once. Cremating a single body has roughly the carbon footprint of a round-trip flight, according to researchers, and composting could largely eliminate those emissions. It also keeps embalming chemicals out of the soil and takes up no permanent cemetery space. That matters because as land prices soar worldwide, burial leases are getting shorter, making a grave a less attractive way to ride out eternity. Terramation also has a spiritual appeal. Instead of harming the planet that sustained us, our final act can be a gift back to it.

Sources indicate that mortality is undergoing a reexamination of sorts as the ultra-rich are trying to cheat death, and AI companies are selling digital avatars of the dead. Terramation offers something humbler: a way to die that actually helps the planet.

#7219. Córdoba’s famous orange trees face a test in one of Spain’s hottest cities

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (965 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Córdoba’s famous orange trees face a test in one of Spain’s hottest cities

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Olive and holm oak leaves kept working at temperatures that damaged orange and tipu, a 17-species test finds, a guide to heat-tolerant trees.
  • Orange trees line the streets and plazas of Córdoba, in southern Spain, and a tree from a warm climate seems like a safe bet for a hot city.
  • In a test of 17 common street and park trees in Córdoba, the orange was among the first to fail in the heat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Olive and holm oak leaves kept working at temperatures that damaged orange and tipu, a 17-species test finds, a guide to heat-tolerant trees.

Orange trees line the streets and plazas of Córdoba, in southern Spain, and a tree from a warm climate seems like a safe bet for a hot city.

In a test of 17 common street and park trees in Córdoba, the orange was among the first to fail in the heat.

Recent findings suggest that the orange tree’s leaves had lost 90% of their photosynthetic function by the time they reached 123°F (50.6°C). Olive leaves held on to 141°F (60.6°C), and holm oak kept working longer than any other species at the halfway mark.

Native Mediterranean and temperate trees tolerated more heat than exotic species from the subtropics, the study found.

The trees were sampled during one week in one city, so the rankings are a starting point rather than a verdict.

Sonia Vega-Rosete and Cristina Bastias of the University of Córdoba ran the test.

Córdoba’s summers already pass 104°F (40°C) on more than 15 days in some months, according to records from AEMET, Spain’s weather agency, and the count is rising.

Street trees cool a city with shade and with the water their leaves release. If heat damages the leaves, both services shrink.

The researchers picked 17 species that are common in Córdoba and span a range of origins. The native Mediterranean trees included olive, holm oak, cork oak and carob.

Ash, white poplar and elm stood in for native temperate trees. The exotics from the subtropics included orange, jacaranda, chinaberry, tipu and catalpa.

In the last week of June 2025, the team cut one sun-exposed branch from each of five mature trees per species, all growing in irrigated city parks.

Back in the lab, they punched leaf discs about 0.6 inches (1.5 centimeters) across and sealed them in bags.

The bags went into a water bath for 30 minutes at each of 11 temperatures, from 77°F to 140°F (25°C to 60°C), six discs per temperature.

Afterward the team measured how well each disc’s light-harvesting machinery still worked.

From those readings, they fitted a curve for each species and read off three thresholds.

The first was the temperature where damage began, and the other two were where half and 90% of function was gone.

Industry observers note that every species held up to about 108°F (42.5°C). Above that, the damage threshold ranged from 108°F for tipu to 125°F (51.5°C) for holm oak.

It has been revealed that the halfway point separated the groups most clearly. Native species lost half their function at an average of about 125°F (51.5°C), exotics at about 121°F (49.6°C).

The gap between the two groups was unlikely to be chance.

For 90% loss, the averages were about 135°F (57.2°C) for natives and 130°F (54.4°C) for exotics.

Grouped by climate of origin, Mediterranean and temperate trees reached about 136°F and 134°F (57.6°C and 56.4°C) before losing 90% of function, and subtropical trees about 128°F (53.5°C).

Whether a tree keeps its leaves in winter made no difference. Evergreen and deciduous species were spread across the rankings.

“This allowed us to identify the temperature thresholds at which the photosynthetic performance of these species begins to be impaired, which could compromise their ability to ‘cool their surroundings,'” Vega-Rosete noted.

The orange tree, chinaberry, catalpa and tipu are planted across Córdoba’s parks and streets, often for their looks or their history there. All four were among the least heat-tolerant trees.

Industry observers note that the authors offer one explanation. A subtropical climate pairs warmth with humidity and plenty of water, and Córdoba supplies the warmth without the other two.

To measure that gap, the team mapped each species’ home climate from occurrence records in GBIF and other databases, matched to climate data from WorldClim.

For the subtropical species, the farther Córdoba’s climate was from the climate of their native range, the lower the temperature at which leaf damage began. Native species highlighted no such drop.

Holm oak, whose native range includes places as hot as Córdoba, had the highest damage threshold of all.

Leaf temperatures matter here. The authors note that leaves can run 14°F to 18°F (8°C to 10°C) hotter than the air around them, and up to 36°F (20°C) hotter in full sun.

A 104°F afternoon can put a leaf past the damage threshold of several of these trees.

It has been revealed that the heat-tolerant trees shared a build. Their wood was denser, their leaves were thicker, and each leaf packed more dry matter into its area.

Species with heavier leaves per unit area lost half their function at higher temperatures, and species with denser wood resisted the onset of damage longer.

Such traits were most pronounced in the native Mediterranean evergreens.

The subtropical exotics, and a few temperate trees such as white poplar and black locust, had the opposite build: bigger leaves with more nitrogen, geared to fast growth.

All of the trees grew in watered parks, so the thresholds may differ for trees on dry streets or in other cities.

The leaves came from a single week of a hot summer. The five trees of each species were pooled, so the test gives one curve per species rather than a range.

The thresholds also capture only one part of how a tree copes with heat. Heat-shock proteins and other chemical defenses weren’t part of the study.

The authors wrote that the same test needs to run in other cities, climates, seasons and years, and on more species, before the rankings can guide planting broadly.

The full study was published in the journal Urban Forestry & Urban Greening.

Whether you’re venturing to the region solo or traveling with friends and family, there are gorgeous options for nearly every type of traveler, each offering a personalized way to visit this corner of the Caribbean. #7217. Why Do Some People Feel Their Souls Leave Their Bodies at Night? The Answer May Lie in a Hidden Brain State.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (913 w)

Why Do Some People Feel Their Souls Leave Their Bodies at Night? The Answer May Lie in a Hidden Brain State.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when you have what is known as an out-of-body experience, you may feel as if your mind has left your body, though it hasn’t actually gone anywhere.
  • To make sense of these intangible phenomena, neuroscientist Teresa Campillo-Ferrer of Radboud University in the Netherlands recruited participants for an experiment designed to capture what happens in the brain when the mind seems to wander from the body during sleep.
  • “Studying UBEs is essential for understanding the mechanisms underlying bodily awareness, self-perception, and the sense of ‘having a body’ (embodiment) or ‘owning a body’ (body ownership),” she wrote in a study recently published in Consciousness and Cognition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when you have what is known as an out-of-body experience, you may feel as if your mind has left your body, though it hasn’t actually gone anywhere. Maybe you feel like you’re floating or flying. On the darker side, it might be an unsettling experience that makes you feel as if your body no longer belongs to you, or a nightmarish bout of sleep paralysis that leaves you panting and in a cold sweat. How can the brain conjure experiences that sound straight out of science fiction but are really nothing more than illusions?

To make sense of these intangible phenomena, neuroscientist Teresa Campillo-Ferrer of Radboud University in the Netherlands recruited participants for an experiment designed to capture what happens in the brain when the mind seems to wander from the body during sleep. Most of her subjects had already had an out-of-body episode or some other kind of unusual bodily experience (UBE). Some were lucid dreamers, people who can become aware that they are dreaming. Others had dealt with sleep paralysis, which is waking up while the body is still paralyzed as it is during dreaming sleep. Some had even felt that they left their physical body behind and passed through a portal to another realm. Although UBEs can occur during waking hours, Campillo-Ferrer reasoned that she would probably capture more of them in sleeping brains.

“Studying UBEs is essential for understanding the mechanisms underlying bodily awareness, self-perception, and the sense of ‘having a body’ (embodiment) or ‘owning a body’ (body ownership),” she wrote in a study recently published in Consciousness and Cognition. “As such, UBE research has the potential to expand current theories of human self-consciousness and multisensory perception.”.

The participants’ main job was simply to relax. Before they drifted off to dreamland, they were fitted with EEG electrodes, practiced pre-sleep meditation, and were given visual stimulation that could help induce lucid dreams and UBEs. Researchers also asked them to move their eyes left and right several times if they noticed anything strange happening, whether or not they were lucid dreaming. This works because even in a semiconscious state, the brain can remember instructions and respond to something unusual. Participants then slept for three hours in soundproof chambers. If the recordings highlighted the left-right eye signal, participants were either spoken to over an intercom or woken up to describe their experiences. After the sleep session ended, participants also discussed their dreams with the researchers.

The reported UBEs fell into several categories. In vestibular-motor experiences, subjects felt as if they were moving or being moved, such as levitating, spinning, or falling. These sensations can also show up in the opposite way, as heaviness or a feeling of sinking deeper and deeper, like the harrowing scene in A Nightmare on Elm Street where Glen is sucked into his own bed. Flying and other movements that defy the laws of physics also belong in this category. In tactile UBEs, the person feels touch or vibrations from an outside source even though nothing is touching them. In UBEs involving distorted body boundaries, the outer limits of the body blur, so that the body seems to merge with the bed (another very Freddy Krueger moment), shapeshift into another form, or gain a duplicate.

Other UBEs are defined by a lack of bodily sensation or sense of position. These are often associated with feeling detached from the physical body or not knowing where the body actually is. They are similar, though not identical, to out-of-body UBEs, in which participants reported leaving their physical body or realizing, at least while dreaming, that they felt separate from it. Because out-of-body experiences often involve a feeling of levitation, they tend to overlap with the vestibular-motor category, though some involve no sense of movement at all. Sleep paralysis made up another category, and it may be the most frightening. The person is fully aware but can’t move, and sometimes it feels as if they can’t breathe. Still other UBEs stemmed from hallucinations or lucid dreams.

Exactly where UBEs arise in the brain is still unknown. After analyzing EEG patterns, however, the researchers suggest that they happen somewhere in the liminal space between waking and sleeping. In participants whose UBEs were confirmed by the eye-movement signal, slower brainwaves known as delta and theta waves decreased while faster beta and gamma waves surged, especially in the temporal lobes on both sides of the brain. These are the regions that process the sensory information that gives us a sense of existing in our bodies. What makes this pattern striking is that slower waves are linked to sleep, while faster waves are more typical of being awake. It is as if the sleeping and waking brain overlap.

It has been revealed that campillo-Ferrer explained the significance of these findings: “Specific EEG features associated with UBEs appear to reflect the reactivation of EEG activity from levels observed in baseline brain states in which UBEs emerge. [Our] models allowed for precise analysis of neural activity and individual variability, providing new insights into the neural correlates associated with UBEs and their role in bodily self-perception and consciousness.”.

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

Exercise may have an overlooked social benefit beyond boosting your mood

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mice with running wheels fought less over food and warmth, suggesting that exercise can influence their social behavior.
  • According to recent reports, exercise is usually recommended for the heart, the lungs, and a better mood.
  • Less fighting over food and a warm resting place was observed in mouse pairs housed with a working running wheel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mice with running wheels fought less over food and warmth, suggesting that exercise can influence their social behavior.

According to recent reports, exercise is usually recommended for the heart, the lungs, and a better mood. In mice, a new study suggests that it may also alter how animals treat one another.

Less fighting over food and a warm resting place was observed in mouse pairs housed with a working running wheel.

Recent findings suggest that pairs whose wheel had been locked fought more often. Greater activity was also recorded in brain areas tied to social behavior among the mice that ran.

Industry observers note that the work was led by Liz Kirby of Ohio State University. She is an associate professor of behavioral neuroscience in the Department of Psychology.

According to recent reports, the findings come from mice and were presented at a scientific meeting. They have not yet appeared in a journal.

“Mice are known to be naturally social. They like hanging out with other mice, just like humans like hanging out with other humans,” Kirby said.

Industry observers note that “They also exercise naturally. If you give them a running wheel, they run about six miles a night, voluntarily.”.

Mice were housed in pairs for six weeks by Kirby’s team. Each pair consisted of two males or two females.

In a recent development, A running wheel was available to some pairs at any hour of the day or night. Other pairs were given a wheel that could not turn.

The same object was therefore present in every cage, yet only one group could run on it.

It has been revealed that each pair was then given something to compete for. A tasty treat was used in one test. In another, the prize was a warm resting spot with room for only one mouse.

The researchers recorded behaviors linked to competitive fighting. These included attempts to steal the food or to push a cage mate off the warm spot.

Sources indicate that according to Kirby, a food pellet was shared more readily by the mice with working wheels. Mice with locked wheels were not as good at sharing it.

“They would rip it from each other’s paws and run away with it in a cage and chase each other down. Generally very rude behavior when it comes to mealtime,” Kirby noted.

A follow-up experiment limited some mice to scheduled wheel sessions. These sessions lasted six hours a day and were held five days a week. Kirby called them visiting the gym.

Sources indicate that the same tests were carried out after six weeks on that schedule. Kirby mentioned that living with a wheel and visiting the gym both seemed to reduce fighting over limited resources.

Constant access to a wheel therefore did not appear necessary for the mice to fight less.

Sources indicate that will Butke is a doctoral student in Kirby’s lab and the lead author of the study. The effects of running inside the brain were also examined by him and his colleagues.

A technique that marks recently active brain cells was used. Some regions linked to social behavior were more active in the mice that ran. Other regions remained unchanged.

“This points toward the idea that this isn’t just a brain-wide increase in activation, but instead that the activation is specifically in certain subregions of the brain,” Butke noted.

Recent findings suggest that these measurements indicate which areas were more active in the running mice. They cannot show whether that activity explains the reduced fighting.

In a recent development, clubs where people exercise together have grown promptly. The fitness app Strava reported that new clubs on its platform nearly quadrupled in 2025.

The total was put at 1 million clubs by Strava. Hiking clubs grew fastest and were followed by running clubs.

Meanwhile, loneliness has worried health officials.

It has been revealed that falling rates of social connection were described as “an urgent public health concern” in a 2023 advisory. It was issued by U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy.

According to Butke, research on what happens in the brain when people exercise socially is limited.

“People like to run in groups or exercise together – not only because you get to have a person you can rely upon, but also it gets you into a social context where you can de-stress,” he said.

Mice and people are difficult to compare directly. Even so, Kirby said the work suggests that exercise has a direct social benefit, since competitive fighting was reduced.

“This adds to the list of potential benefits you could be getting by exercising,” Kirby said.

“It’s not just going to make your heart healthier, and it’s not just going to reduce your risk for cancer, obesity and stroke, but it also might help strengthen your social ties.”.

It has been revealed that A poster is an early step, and a full paper has not yet been released. The number of mice tested and the brain regions that changed would be detailed in that paper.

All of the mice lived in pairs, so the results describe exercise with a companion nearby. The behavior of a mouse that runs alone remains a separate question.

Future research could test whether exercise changes how people share and compete, as it did in these mice.

The work was presented on November 18 as a poster at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.

#7213. Breaking: Locusts may help scientists detect hard-to-treat lung infections

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1216 w)
📖 Baca

Breaking: Locusts may help scientists detect hard-to-treat lung infections

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1216 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In lab tests, locusts could smell the difference between bacterial biofilms and free-floating bacteria, a finding that could inform future breath tests.
  • Bacteria become much harder to kill once they attach to a surface and build a slimy protective layer.
  • No test can at the moment detect them in a patient’s lungs without an invasive procedure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In lab tests, locusts could smell the difference between bacterial biofilms and free-floating bacteria, a finding that could inform future breath tests.

Bacteria become much harder to kill once they attach to a surface and build a slimy protective layer.

These colonies are called biofilms. No test can at the moment detect them in a patient’s lungs without an invasive procedure.

A locust’s sense of smell might help one day.

In lab tests, researchers used signals from locust brains to tell biofilms apart from free-floating bacteria of the same species by smell.

The clearest signal appeared about a second after the odor reached the locusts’ antennae.

Debajit Saha and Jonathan Hardy were the senior authors of the study. Both are associate professors at Michigan State University (MSU). Michael Parnas was the first author.

According to recent reports, saha works in the College of Engineering. Hardy is based in the Department of Microbiology, Genetics and Immunology. Both researchers also belong to MSU’s Institute for Quantitative Health Science and Engineering.

According to recent reports, only bacterial cultures grown in flasks were used. Breath samples and patients were not tested.

Saha noted that before the experiments, it was not clear that an odor alone could show how bacteria were growing.

“Seeing such a high level of discrimination was therefore quite surprising,” Saha said.

A biofilm forms when bacteria settle on a solid surface. A sticky coating is then built around the whole colony.

Sources indicate that inside that coating, bacteria can be up to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics than free-floating bacteria. The authors gave that figure in the paper.

Industry observers note that some bacteria deep in the colony have a slower metabolism. Those cells can survive treatment, and the biofilm is rebuilt afterward.

Industry observers note that biofilms account for about 80% of bacterial infections in people, according to earlier research cited in the paper. Wounds, implants and the lungs can all be affected.

It has been revealed that an infection is usually identified by growing a sample in a laboratory. That process takes a few days. Faster tests exist, but they cannot separate a biofilm from free-floating bacteria.

Bacteria also release chemicals into the air as they grow. Together, those airborne chemicals form an odor. An odor can be sampled from outside the body.

Locusts smell with their antennae. More than 100,000 odor-sensing nerve cells are found on each antenna.

The signals from those cells all pass through about 800 output neurons. These neurons are located in one small smell-processing region of the brain.

For the experiment, the brain was surgically exposed in six living locusts. Each insect was held still, and an electrode was placed in that region.

The team then blew air from five flasks across the antennae. Four flasks contained bacteria. The fifth contained only the broth in which the bacteria had been grown.

Two species were used, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Each species was grown in two ways, as a biofilm and as a free-floating culture.

Each odor was delivered for four seconds and repeated five times, with one minute between deliveries. The activity of 32 neurons was isolated from the recordings.

The locusts had not been trained on these odors. Insect brains have been used this way by Saha’s lab before. In earlier work, recordings were taken from locusts and honeybees exposed to the odors of human cancer cells.

Trained dogs can also detect some diseases by smell. However, a test based on an animal’s behavior gives only a yes or a no, the authors wrote.

According to recent reports, A computer program compared the firing pattern from each trial with the patterns from the other trials. The closest match was then selected.

It has been revealed that when all five odors were included, 22 of 25 trials were matched to the correct flask. That is an accuracy of 88%. Guessing would be right only 20% of the time.

Both biofilms were identified in every trial.

One of the five free-floating Staphylococcus trials was mistaken for the Staphylococcus biofilm. The plain broth was also mistaken for a Staphylococcus odor twice.

Sources indicate that in this analysis, every biofilm was caught by the program. One free-floating sample was wrongly flagged as a biofilm, however.

The researchers reported accuracy of up to 96% when individual biofilm and free-floating odors were classified.

The largest differences in firing patterns were seen between the two species. Biofilm and free-floating cultures of the same species produced more similar patterns. Even so, they were still separated by the recordings.

Saha stated bacteria release a different mix of airborne chemicals when their growth state changes. These subtle changes can be picked up by the insects.

In a recent development, before the odor arrived, the program performed no better than guessing. Accuracy rose quickly once the odor was delivered.

Sources indicate that the team then tested how little brain activity was needed. A half-second slice of the recording was enough for 91% accuracy. That slice was centered about one second after the odor arrived.

A quarter-second slice from the same moment gave 82% accuracy. A laboratory culture, by comparison, takes days.

It has been revealed that the 32 neurons represent about 4% of the roughly 800 output neurons in the smell-processing region. The biofilm analysis was also repeated on random subsets of the 32.

Performance improved as more neurons were included.

Sources indicate that only one laboratory strain of each species was used. Human breath is more complicated. It also carries chemicals from food, medications and the surrounding air.

It has been revealed that several other limits were listed by the authors. The number of bacteria could not be kept exactly equal in the biofilm and free-floating flasks. That difference alone could change an odor.

Industry observers note that all 32 neurons were pooled from six insects. The study therefore does not show a single locust doing the job.

Recent findings suggest that the recordings stayed strong for about four hours after surgery. How long a locust lasts as a sensor depends on its health and the surgeon’s skill, the authors wrote.

Drug-resistant strains such as MRSA were not tested either. The team expects those strains to be harder to distinguish from ordinary Staphylococcus.

No one has yet tested whether a locust brain can pick a biofilm’s odor out of human breath.

Breath studies are the next step, the authors wrote. Hardy noted the team is interested in testing breath samples from children with cystic fibrosis. Persistent lung infections that involve biofilms can develop in these children.

Pseudomonas is a major cause of lung infections in people with the disease, according to the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation.

Custom electrodes are also being developed so that enough data can be collected from a single locust.

In the long term, the researchers want to build a portable sensor. It would connect a living locust’s smell system to small electronics and artificial intelligence.

More bacterial species and samples from patients will be needed in future work. The results will also have to be compared with the laboratory methods already used in hospitals.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if there’s one thing I take almost as seriously as chasing some good snow, it’s having the right wardrobe to go with it. I’m a lifelong snowboarder, a fairly recent convert to skiing, and someone who has spent plenty of winters bouncing between mountains on the east coast and out west. I’ve learned that the best of the best ski gear needs to do a lot more than look good in a lodge photo. It has to hold up through long lift rides, changing conditions, unexpected snowfall, and the occasional unglamorous tumble.

According to recent reports, but that doesn’t mean style needs to take a backseat. In fact, I’d argue that the two should go hand in hand. That's a massive part of why the popular ski brand, Halfdays, first caught my attention three years ago—and why I keep coming back season after season. Founded in 2020 by former Olympic freestyle aerial skier Kiley McKinnon and Ariana Ferweda, Halfdays came onto the ski scene with a refreshing take: women's ski apparel that actually considers women. Not just smaller versions of men’s gear or the usual boxy, so-called unisex silhouettes, but (finally) thoughtfully designed outerwear that takes fit, function, and fashion all very seriously.

Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is wearing the Halfdays Ashton jacket and Alessandra pant in Stowe, Vermont.

Recent findings suggest that the outdoor apparel industry has come a long way, but finding technical pieces that feel just as considered aesthetically as they are functional on the mountain can still be a bit of a treasure hunt. So as someone who has accumulated her fair share of ski and snowboard gear over the years, I immediately fell in love with the brand’s mission, and eventually, the gear itself.

While I’ve come to adore its ski suits, bibs, and winter jackets, Halfdays' assortment has expanded beyond the big-ticket ski uniform. The brand offers sweat-wicking baselayers, cozy fleeces, everyday outdoor staples, and chic accessories that make sense well beyond your stay at a ski resort. My favorite pieces from Halfdays keep me feeling comfortable and put together on harsh winter days in New York City too, from knit headbands that cover my ears to winter leggings and warm socks that aren’t too thick.

Sources indicate that of course, Halfdays isn’t the same brand it was when I first discovered it. What began as a ski-focused label has evolved into an outdoor brand with spring and summer collections spanning hiking, running, and more warm-weather pursuits. Its arrival at major retailers like Nordstrom, REI, and Backcountry, the opening of its Denver flagship (along with plenty of other storefronts), and a string of collaborations have helped solidify it as a functional brand for every outdoor adventurer.

Chapel is wearing the Parks Projects x Halfdays set on the slopes in Park City, Utah.

According to recent reports, that remarked, the brand has been having some fun with its fashion credentials, most recently teaming up with Gigi Hadid’s Guest in Residence on an eight-piece winter capsule. The result is a nostalgic take on mountainwear, bringing Guest in Residence’s signature knitwear looks to Halfdays' mountain-ready vibes, with playful retro details that feel just as at home at après-ski as they do on the slopes.

On the performance side, though, I’m excited about the brand’s newest launch: Halfdays has officially joined forces with Gore-Tex for its most technical outerwear collection yet. From down jackets and shells to bibs and mittens, the colorful collection brings together trusted waterproof, windproof, and breathable technology with the fit and design that initially made me fall for Halfdays in the first place.

As another winter of snow chasing commences, I’m giving my cold-weather wardrobe yet another Halfdays refresh. Below, my tried-and-true ski season favorites from Halfdays, along with a few winter staples I’ve got my eye on.

The Lawrence jacket is designed with Primaloft insulation, keeping you warm on the coldest winter days. It features underarm vents and an exterior chest pocket with an attached phone leash. Plus, the hood is adjustable, so you’ll get a perfect fit over your helmet every time. The jacket is best for bluebird days given its cropped length, but it’s also available in a longer version too.

In a recent development, I like to pair the Lawrence jacket with these matching shell pants. With a slim fit, an adjustable waistband, a water-resistant exterior, and zippered hems for snow boots, this pair is just as practical as it is stylish. Pro tip: Try these bad boys on with a pair of your favorite winter leggings underneath before hitting the mountain, just so you know that you’ll be comfortable and warm all day long.

Don’t underestimate the importance of a solid baselayer. The Johnson top features mesh underarms and a sweat-wicking finish, so you don’t have to worry about overheating in your ski gear. The long-sleeve layer also has a silicon grip on the inside hem, preventing it from sliding up as you move.

Pair the Johnson top with these leggings for a stylish, mountain-ready set. They’re sweat-wicking and feature a layer of mesh on the calves for added breathability. Even better, they’re versatile enough to wear off the mountain too, whether you’re shopping at a holiday market or strolling through the park.

Made with 100% merino wool, this chic Jacquard headband will keep your head and ears warm on the slopes—and it tastefully reps the brand too. I have (and love) it in the color Blue Fog, but it’s also available in black and red.

Industry observers note that I’m obsessed with these Gore-Tex x Halfdays mittens. Along with the insulated, breathable, and waterproof design, there’s also a leather palm construction for added grip and durability.

I can’t wait to put this three-layer shell jacket to the test on my trip to Stowe, Vermont, this December. It has all the classic Gore-Tex technologies that make the collaboration so enticing in the first place: engineered with durable water- and wind-proof material, and breathable protection without added insulation.

For a matching set, grab this three-layer shell bib constructed with the same Gore-Tex build. With adjustable shoulder straps, a drop-seat construction, thigh vents, and gusseted hems, you’ll be covered and ready for anything, from head to toe.

Ah, one of the early Halfday classics. The tried-and-true Ashton jacket does it all, from ski trips to cabin getaways. With an adjustable (and removable) belt buckle enclosure, a helmet hood, and its many pockets for your phone and ski pass, it offers every bit of function you need for a full day on the mountain.

Recent findings suggest that for those who favor a puffy yet packable one-piece, the Murphy ski suit is another one of Halfdays' original bestsellers. I own this bad boy in red, and wear it when I need extra warmth on the mountain. One thing to note: I’m 5'3", and it’s just a bit long on my legs when I’m not in snow boots—but it’s not very often that I wear the suit without them.

While I haven’t shopped the new Guest in Residence collection yet, I’m eyeing this chic ski sweater that looks straight out of a ’70s après-ski scene. I can already picture myself wearing it post-slopes, sipping on a spiked cider at the ski lodge.

For another vintage-inspired piece from the Guest in Residence collection, this cable knit inspired down jacket is all about staying warm in style. (And I’ve already added it to my cart.).

Recent findings suggest that get your hands on one of the Parks Project x Halfdays ski jackets while you still can. This gorgeous print is inspired by the Rocky Mountains—and I always receive compliments from other shredders when I wear it out on the slopes. Not to mention, it keeps me warm and comfy while doing so!

#7210. Eagles may hunt baboons as heavy as some early human relatives

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1308 w)

Eagles may hunt baboons as heavy as some early human relatives

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1308 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Punctured baboon skulls found beneath cliffs in Chad suggest Verreaux’s eagles may hunt larger primates than scientists once thought possible.
  • Industry observers note that eagles are known to kill monkeys.
  • According to recent reports, that view is now challenged by skulls of adult male olive baboons found below desert cliffs in the Sahara.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Punctured baboon skulls found beneath cliffs in Chad suggest Verreaux’s eagles may hunt larger primates than scientists once thought possible.

Industry observers note that eagles are known to kill monkeys. A full-grown male baboon, however, has long been considered too heavy for any bird to take.

According to recent reports, that view is now challenged by skulls of adult male olive baboons found below desert cliffs in the Sahara. The damage on them suggests that Verreaux’s eagles can kill such animals anyway.

Industry observers note that A hole was punched through the bone of the eye socket in each skull. It is the kind of wound that an eagle’s talon leaves. One of the baboons weighed an estimated 48 pounds (21.8 kg).

If the researchers are right, an eagle can kill prey as heavy as some early human relatives.

The study was led by Catherine Hobaiter of the University of St Andrews. She worked with colleagues at Dartmouth College, the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, and African Parks.

No one on the team saw an eagle attack a baboon. The case rests on bones.

Recent findings suggest that three sites on the Ennedi Plateau were visited by the team in February and March 2025. The plateau is a sandstone landscape in northeastern Chad.

Among the fallen rock below its cliffs, the skulls of two adult male baboons were found at two different sites.

Neither puncture showed signs of healing, so the damage could have occurred around the time of death or afterward.

“We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Hobaiter said.

“Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”.

The right shoulder blade of the first male had been punctured and scraped as well. Eagles leave that pattern when they open a body to reach the heart and lungs.

According to recent reports, the team also needed to know how heavy the baboons were. The ball at the top of each thigh bone was therefore measured in scaled photographs.

An established formula for monkeys converts that width into an estimate of body weight.

In a recent development, both thigh bones were found with the first punctured skull. From them, the team estimated that male’s weight at about 48 pounds (21.8 kg).

These weights matter because of a rule of thumb in research on primates and their predators. Primates under 29 pounds (13 kg) are known eagle prey. No heavier primate has ever been confirmed as an eagle’s kill.

Sources indicate that primates between 29 and 44 pounds (13 and 20 kg) are treated as vulnerable in theory. Anything heavier is assumed to be safe from birds.

A third punctured skull was recovered on a return trip in June 2026, along with part of the skeleton. This male weighed an estimated 58 pounds (26.2 kg), and both of his shoulder blades had been scraped.

He was at least twice as heavy as any primate confirmed as eagle prey.

According to recent reports, in all, thigh bones were collected from nine baboons. Eight were adult males with an average estimated weight of 49 pounds (22.2 kg).

Industry observers note that A hole in a baboon’s skull does not have to come from an eagle. Other causes were therefore considered by the team.

Recent findings suggest that A gunshot would be expected to do much more damage to the skull, and none was found. Male baboons also kill each other with their canine teeth. Such fights tend to leave crushed bone and extra tooth gouges, yet the skulls had neither.

According to recent reports, verreaux’s eagles are known to dive at baboons that come near their nests. No nest was found above or near the skulls, however.

One possibility was harder to dismiss. Verreaux’s eagles sometimes eat dead animals. The scraped shoulder blade could be explained by an eagle pulling apart a carcass.

In a recent development, the authors wrote that this cannot be definitively ruled out. Two reasons to doubt it were given.

It has been revealed that first, the skull punctures are far more severe than the shallow pits seen in an earlier experiment. In that experiment, a golden eagle had gripped a dead monkey.

Second, nearly all the bones came from adult males. An eagle that feeds on carcasses would be expected to eat a dead baboon of either sex.

“At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t,” noted Nathaniel Dominy of Dartmouth, the study’s senior author.

An eagle does not have to lift its prey to kill it. Golden eagles land on the back of a hoofed animal and hold on until it collapses. Similar methods are used by Verreaux’s eagles.

Verreaux’s eagles also hunt in pairs. The prey is startled by one bird, and the other attacks from below to force it off the cliff.

The grip of a Verreaux’s eagle can span up to 16 inches (40 cm). That is more than twice the width of an adult male baboon’s skull.

Recent findings suggest that the Ennedi baboons appear to spend much of the day on vertical cliff faces. Some are as tall as 490 feet (150 meters).

Water and palm fruit are found on the canyon floor, but it offers little shade or shelter.

In a recent development, when young baboons are threatened by an eagle, the males bark and lunge at it. The team suggested that this could make males more likely to be killed on a cliff.

On June 19, 2026, the researchers watched a pair of Verreaux’s eagles.

The birds flew along a cliff where baboons were resting. Several baboons gave alarm calls, and those in exposed spots dropped swiftly to shelter.

“We’d seen them very relaxed around other substantial birds of prey, but as soon as the Verreaux came into view they alarm called and dropped down to safety,” Hobaiter remarked.

The argument reaches past baboons because of a famous fossil. In 1995, researchers argued that the Taung Child had been killed by an eagle.

The Taung Child was a young early human relative.

Recent findings suggest that the punctures in the Ennedi skulls resemble the damage to that fossil’s eye socket. The Taung Child, however, weighed an estimated 22 to 26 pounds (10 to 12 kg) at most.

That weight falls inside the accepted limit for eagle prey.

Research on what hunted larger early human relatives has focused on mammals, especially big cats. Hobaiter’s team argued that eagles deserve attention too.

If eagles can kill adult baboons this large, the authors argue that some early human relatives may also have been vulnerable.

Monkeys defend themselves differently against eagles than against cats, and males often step in during eagle attacks.

Recent findings suggest that several traits could have been shaped by pressure from eagles, the authors wrote. These include the size difference between males and females, cooperation among males, and infant care.

That part of the argument was called speculative by the authors.

Three punctured skulls point to possible eagle attacks, and baboons sounded alarm calls when a pair of Verreaux’s eagles flew past.

The researchers have yet to see one of these eagles attack an adult baboon.

Nearly all the bones came from adult males, and the authors called that pattern puzzling.

3D scans of the bones have been posted in public archives by the researchers, where others can examine the punctures.

Future fieldwork at Ennedi could show whether eagles kill adult male baboons there, and how often.

The full study was published in the journal American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

#7208. Tech Report: NASA's Voyager 1 mission forever changed our view of Jupiter

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (820 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Livescience ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: NASA's Voyager 1 mission forever changed our view of Jupiter

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a latest milestone.
  • While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune.
  • One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a latest milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Sources indicate that voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Recent findings suggest that this discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

In a recent development, taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency declared its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.
