#7207. Thanksgiving food waste can start before the turkey even goes in the oven

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1415 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Thanksgiving food waste can start before the turkey even goes in the oven

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1415 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans wasted about 166,000 metric tons of food during Thanksgiving week in 2025, roughly 39% more than during a comparison week.
  • When Thanksgiving food waste comes up, leftovers usually get the blame.
  • Industry observers note that the stuffing went unfinished, or half a pie stayed on the counter until Sunday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans wasted about 166,000 metric tons of food during Thanksgiving week in 2025, roughly 39% more than during a comparison week.

When Thanksgiving food waste comes up, leftovers usually get the blame.

Industry observers note that the stuffing went unfinished, or half a pie stayed on the counter until Sunday. In some homes, though, good food is discarded before the meal is even cooked. It is thrown out so a shelf can be cleared for the turkey.

Researchers documented this habit in surveys of U.S. households around Thanksgiving 2025. More edible food was discarded by those households in the holiday week than in a later, ordinary week.

In a recent development, extra waste was reported by cooks who emptied the fridge to make room. Cooks who had to guess their guests’ appetites reported more too, compared with cooks who made just enough.

The researchers therefore see the days before the meal as a chance to cut holiday waste.

According to recent reports, ran Li of Penn State University and Brian Roe of Ohio State University carried out the surveys. Roe is a professor of agricultural, environmental and development economics.

In a recent development, all of the figures are based on people’s own reports about their kitchens. Nobody’s trash was actually weighed.

Industry observers note that “There’s not a lot of great data out there about which holidays cause the most waste,” Roe mentioned. “My money would be on Thanksgiving because it is so focused around the meal – it is the big tradition.”.

Household waste surveys normally skip holiday weeks, since researchers are after a typical week. Yearly totals based on such surveys therefore miss the holidays.

Sources indicate that for this study, 879 adults were surveyed before and after Thanksgiving 2025. Every one of them handled at least half of the cooking at home.

In a recent development, about a week after the first survey, they reported how much food their households had not eaten. That included anything thrown out, composted or fed to pets.

Bones, peels and pits were left out of the count. Only once-edible food was included.

Later, in December, 437 of the same households repeated the exercise for a non-holiday week.

Households that reported in both weeks discarded about 1.1 pounds (500 grams) of edible food per person during Thanksgiving week.

About 0.8 pounds (358 grams) was discarded in the December week. The Thanksgiving total was therefore 39% higher.

People who skipped the holiday meal discarded about the same amount in both weeks.

According to recent reports, the results were then scaled up to the whole country. By the authors’ estimate, Americans discarded about 367 million pounds (166,000 metric tons) of edible food during Thanksgiving week.

That amounts to roughly a pound for every person in the United States.

Based on respondents’ estimates, Americans wasted about $3 billion worth of edible food during Thanksgiving week, roughly 40% more than during the December comparison week.

“That’s a pretty healthy chunk of change, particularly as people are concerned about high food prices right now,” Roe stated.

Four out of five respondents took part in a Thanksgiving meal as a host, a guest or both.

About 0.8 pounds (356 grams) per person was discarded that week by people who neither hosted nor attended a meal.

Guests who did not host averaged 1.2 pounds (545 grams). Hosts who did not attend another meal averaged 1.1 pounds (493 grams).

The highest average, 1.8 pounds (818 grams), was reported by respondents who hosted one meal and attended another. That is more than double the amount for people who skipped the holiday.

These gaps remained after age, income, household size and shopping habits were taken into account.

Sources indicate that the meal was not blamed for all of that week’s waste. About a quarter of the discarded food was tied by respondents to hosting or attending a Thanksgiving meal.

Recent findings suggest that different foods were also thrown out by hosts and guests. More meat, turkey included, was discarded by hosts than by guests. Half of the people who only attended a meal had cooked a dish at home to bring.

About 500 respondents cooked for a Thanksgiving meal, either as hosts or as guests bringing a dish. Of those cooks, 74% mentioned they had deliberately made more food than was needed.

Sources indicate that the cooks gave three main reasons. Leftovers were the goal for the largest group, 37% of the cooks. Another 25% did not know how much their guests would eat. A further 12% mentioned a big spread was the tradition.

In a recent development, each of these groups reported more waste than cooks who tried to make just enough. Leftover planners reported about 0.4 pounds (189 grams) more per person for the week.

Cooks who were unsure reported about 0.8 pounds (363 grams) more.

A proposal for the extra food was thus associated with less waste than a guess was.

For cooks who guess, tools such as the Guest-Imator were suggested by Li and Roe. It is a calculator from the Natural Resources Defense Council.

A guest count and the amount of leftovers wanted are entered, and the calculator returns quantities to buy.

A use for the extra food was found by many cooks. Among hosts, 37% sent guests home with leftovers. About one in six respondents with leftovers froze some.

Industry observers note that the cooks were also asked about the days before the meal. Had food been thrown away to make room for the turkey and the other holiday groceries?

About one in five cooks said yes.

According to recent reports, nearly a pound (438 grams) more waste per person was reported for the week by cooks who cleared space. The comparison was with meal participants who neither cleared space nor cooked too much.

That extra amount alone exceeds the 0.8 pounds reported for the whole week by a person who skipped Thanksgiving.

“They would clear out a bunch of stuff,” Roe noted.

Sources indicate that li and Roe wrote that campaigns before the holiday could help. One example they gave was recipes that use up fridge items the night before the turkey is bought.

“Think about what’s in the fridge that can be used up before the turkey’s coming in so that you can have that place for all your fixings for the holiday meal,” he stated.

Respondents also reported where the food went: the trash, the compost or the sink.

During Thanksgiving week, 98% more food per person went down the sink or garbage disposal than in December.

It has been revealed that residents of some cities are warned around the holidays about fatbergs. These are buildups of fat, oil and grease that can damage sewer pipes.

The kind of food that went down the drain was not recorded. However, 85% more meat and fish was discarded during Thanksgiving week by households that reported in both weeks.

Li and Roe suspect that holiday cooking adds fat, oil and grease to what goes down the sink.

Because the study is a survey, it shows which habits were associated with more waste. It cannot show that any single habit caused the waste.

The respondents were drawn from an online research panel. Their answers were adjusted to match U.S. households on age, income and household size. Even so, the respondents were not a random sample.

In earlier research, surveys of this kind found 32% to 52% less waste than physical measurement of household waste did. The national totals may therefore be underestimates.

Each household’s waste was also divided by the number of people who normally live there. The number of people at the table was not used. A host’s figure therefore looks bigger, and a guest’s figure looks smaller.

Only about half of the Thanksgiving respondents reported again in December.

Recent findings suggest that for some of them, the December week ended just before Christmas. That week may not have been an ordinary one either.

In a recent development, the survey also did not test any solution. It remains unknown if a portion calculator or a night of use-it-up cooking reduces what is thrown out.

According to Li and Roe, household waste should be weighed over a holiday in future studies.

They also recommended that similar surveys be run for other food-centered holidays.

The full study was published in the journal Waste.

#7205. This magic mushroom can kill

This magic mushroom can kill

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.
  • The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

It has been revealed that that species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik states. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

In a recent development, related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

Industry observers note that the small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding reveals that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” notes Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Industry observers note that discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve newly introduced traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

In a recent development, ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

In a recent development, the two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a upcoming mushroom, Pringle indicates. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

#7204. Tech Report: Offshore wind turbines may reshape the low clouds around them

Tech Report: Offshore wind turbines may reshape the low clouds around them

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clouds can change how much electricity offshore wind farms produce, while turbines can also thin low clouds nearby.
  • Low clouds over the sea do more than just block sunlight.
  • This moving air also affects the wind turbines below.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clouds can change how much electricity offshore wind farms produce, while turbines can also thin low clouds nearby.

Low clouds over the sea do more than just block sunlight. The tops of these clouds lose heat to space, which cools the air and keeps it moving.

This moving air also affects the wind turbines below.

In computer simulations, turbines in the last rows produced about 11% more power when the air above the clouds was drier than when it was moister.

The wind turbines also affected the clouds. When the clouds were low enough to touch the turbine blades, the turbines made them thinner over several miles in the direction of the wind.

Clouds are left out of many simulations of offshore wind farms.

It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Twente in the Netherlands put them in. Their results suggest that planners of large offshore farms should take clouds into account.

All of this was tested in computer simulations, not at real wind farms.

The clouds in question are stratocumulus. These low, lumpy sheets are the most common cloud type on Earth.

Industry observers note that in an average year, they cover about 25% to 30% of the North Sea. Wind energy projects are widespread there, and more are planned.

Recent findings suggest that the North Sea is cloudy so often that its wind farms’ energy output may be affected, said Davide Selvatici. Selvatici is a postdoctoral researcher in the university’s Physics of Fluids group.

In a recent development, modelers had often worked with idealized skies that held almost no cloud, said Richard Stevens. Stevens is a professor of fluid mechanics at Twente.

In a recent development, thijs van den Ham, a co-author, mentioned wind farm simulations need clouds in them. “They do play a role, and they do matter,” the author added.

According to recent reports, humidity by itself doesn’t do much to a turbine. Moist air and dry air differ in density by less than 1%. Power output changes by about the same amount.

So the team looked at how clouds change the air’s motion. An earlier study by Selvatici and Stevens had already examined this. In that work, the slowed wind behind a simulated farm recovered faster under low clouds.

The simulations were detailed enough to follow individual gusts and swirls of air.

In a recent development, the work was done in two stages. Cloud layers were first simulated without any turbines, and the temperature and moisture of the overlying air were varied. About 300 simulated hours passed before each of those layers reached a steady state.

A wind farm was then added beneath a selection of those cloud layers. It had 60 turbines in 10 staggered rows, and each was rated at 10 megawatts.

Rotors measured 585 feet (178 meters) across, which put the blade tips 682 feet (208 meters) above the water.

The Washington Monument is shorter than that. At such a height, the blades could reach into the lowest simulated clouds.

A block of air 37 miles (60 kilometers) long surrounded the farm in the model. The block was divided into more than 560 million cells.

Two sets of runs were carried out so that the cloud’s effect could be separated from the effect of moisture.

Industry observers note that cooling at the cloud top was held fixed in the first set. In the second set, cooling was allowed to respond to the moisture overhead, which is how real clouds behave.

Sources indicate that when cooling was held fixed, the drier and moister cases differed by about 3% in power from the last rows. A gap that small lies within the uncertainty of the simulations.

Once cooling was allowed to respond, the same comparison produced a difference of 11%.

The cloud itself was responsible for the larger difference, according to the team’s analysis.

Industry observers note that heat is emitted upward by a cloud top, while water vapor in the overlying air radiates heat back down. Less heat is returned by drier air, so the top of the cloud cools more rapidly.

Sources indicate that that stronger cooling stirred the air underneath more vigorously and the cloud-topped layer deepened. As a result, more of the wind’s energy was transported downward into the farm.

Energy arriving from above is most important at the back of a wind farm.

Recent findings suggest that more than half of the power in the front rows comes from wind that flows in. Each row, however, leaves slower air in its wake for the rows that follow.

In the final rows of the simulated farm, turbulent mixing supplied up to about 90% of a row’s power.

In a recent development, A second effect appeared when the air above the cloud was moister. The cloud-topped layer was then shallower and the approaching wind was slowed more strongly ahead of the farm. The first row of turbines produced less power as a consequence.

Temperature was also found to matter. In the runs with fixed cooling, the researchers varied the temperature contrast between the sea surface and the air above.

Recent findings suggest that the air temperature was taken about 2 miles (3 kilometers) up. The farm’s output then differed by about 20% from a reference case.

Satellite images had already suggested that wind farms affect clouds.

Sources indicate that on two mornings, June 5, 2016, and November 14, 2022, North Sea wind farms were photographed by NASA’s Terra satellite. The images indicated partly cleared cloud near clusters of wind farms. The team took them from NASA Worldview.

Sources indicate that the simulated thinning was strongest under two conditions. The base of the cloud was near the blade tips, and the cloud held little liquid water.

Recent findings suggest that in the run with the lowest cloud, the cloud layer’s top was 587 feet (179 meters) above the sea. That is below the blade tips.

Behind the farm, that cloud held up to 85% less liquid water than in a matching run without turbines.

Recent findings suggest that warmer, drier air from above was mixed into the cloud by turbulence from the turbines. More of the cloud’s water evaporated.

Ahead of the farm, the cloud changed the opposite way.

The wind slowed as it approached the first row. In that same run, the cloud there held up to about 43% more liquid water than the incoming cloud.

The authors compared that to the Horns Rev wind farm. There, slowing wind ahead of the turbines has been linked to fog forming upwind.

According to recent reports, every run was set in the daytime, with the sun at a fixed angle. Sunlight weakens a low cloud, and the authors wrote that daytime conditions may have amplified the thinning.

The simulations also had no rain, a single farm layout, and the same large-scale wind in every run.

The simulated clouds thinned in the same general way as the photographed ones. The amounts were not compared.

Sources indicate that large clusters of wind farms weren’t simulated either. The authors wrote that those need more observations and more modeling.

Next, the team aims to simulate more kinds of weather and larger farms spaced farther apart. Selvatici noted that simulating real weather conditions will take more computing power than is available now.

The full study was published in the Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy.

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in Upcoming York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best hotels in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here, and the best resorts in the Caribbean here.

Turks and Caicos’s bustling yet beautiful island of Providenciales (affectionately dubbed “Provo”) has had its moment in the proverbial sun. Consider venturing southeast to South Caicos for a more intimate and undeveloped look at what are arguably the Caribbean’s most jaw-dropping beaches. The first property to put down literal roots with nearly 800 acres of primarily local vegetation is Sailrock South Caicos: a stunning, 40-unit property on the southeastern island’s northern tip where the Atlantic Ocean and Caicos Bank converge to house the area’s latest and greatest escape. Travel to South Caicos is also more convenient than ever with two direct flights from Miami on Wednesdays and Sundays via American Airlines. This means guests can now bypass a layover in Providenciales and reach paradise in less than two hours.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

At the Ritz-Carlton Turks and Caicos, guests can sandwich sun-soaked days of lounging in a private cabana or on Grace Bay’s idyllic slice of beach with plenty of on-site experiences. A favorite for its white-sand beachfront and unrivaled centrality on famed Grace Bay, there’s no shortage of pursuits here—it’s a choose-your-own-adventure property with great amenities for young kids. 147 luxury ocean-view rooms and suites—with the Ritz-Carlton standard—awe and delight. There’s also a collection of luxury residences and penthouses for longer stays, each, of course, with stunning floor-to-ceiling views of Grace Bay’s turquoise waters. Interiors are all creams and whites with gentle pops of beachy colors, large windows, and pristine linens. As the most central property in Grace Bay, everything is within walking distance: the best restaurants, shops, and even a grocery store. For families with little ones, the Ritz Kids club is the place to be for guests ages 4–12. Drop the kids off and embark on the resort’s luxury sailing catamaran, the Lady Grace.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Salterra balances solitude and serenity with grace. Backgrounding the sprawling complex is a skirt of rugged cliffs and leafy tropical flora—the stuff of our beach getaway daydreams. With staff-organized excursions across the gin-clear Caribbean, a seaside garden sprinkled with lounge chairs begging for sunbathers, and a state-of-the-art spa with eight treatment rooms, whether you're up for an adventure or down for a little R&R, the choice is truly yours. While the island is only home to 1,100 total residents, guests in search of an even greater sense of privacy can book private cabanas looking over the four sun-lit pools that bleed into the horizon.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

It has been revealed that basking on a coveted stretch of Grace Bay, this well-appointed resort is as lax as it is luxe. While there’s plenty of opportunities for R&R at the blissful on-site spa and for romance to blossom over candlelit dinners, the Sands at Grace Bay also know a thing or two about picking up speed. It wouldn’t be a proper Turks and Caicos vacation without hitting the water, and the resort provides complimentary access to a variety of water sport equipment ranging from sea kayaks to snorkeling gear to explore the mirror-clear seas. If you’re traveling with little ones who aren’t quite ready for the open ocean yet, there’s also kid-friendly pools and sprawling perfect for their next adventure. If you’re looking for a resort that grows up alongside your family, look no further.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

It has been revealed that wymara Resort + Villas sits on the western curve of Grace Bay in Providenciales, just a 10-minute drive from the airport. It’s a place for travelers who like their luxury understated and favor the clean lines of minimalist design. Rooms and suites open to sea views and sun-washed balconies, while the villas—set apart from the main resort on a 15-acre peninsula—offer private pools, over-water decks, and personal hosts. The food is sustainably sourced: Indigo serves refined Caribbean dishes, and the Pink Bar is a magnet for sunset watchers. The spa, using island-grown botanicals and 111SKIN products, is intimate and calm. Service is polished yet relaxed, with staff who are friendly and will remember your preferences. Eco credentials are strong, from solar-powered electricity to refillable amenities. Complimentary wellness activities include yoga, pilates, HIIT, and sound baths, while evening entertainment leans local and cultural.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

This mega-resort sets itself apart from other all-inclusive properties throughout the region with its family-friendly activities. There is a 45,000-square-foot waterpark and kids clubs for different ages, including one with Caribbean-ified Sesame Street characters, the Xbox Play Lounge, and a teen disco. For the rest of the family, there are 10 swimming pools, 21 restaurants, 15 bars (some of them swim-up), and access to the 12-mile Grace Bay Beach. The 758 rooms and suites are spread across five themed villages, with architecture that represents different regions: France, Italy, the Caribbean, and Key West. With 43 room categories, the resort truly offers something for everyone.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

In a recent development, grace Bay Club offers not one, but three distinct accommodations to its discerning guests: the adults-only Hotel building, the family-friendly Villas Suites, and the Estate, a resort within a resort, with exclusive access to dedicated amenities, such as a separate pool, cabanas, and more. Despite catering to different crowds, they do have a few common features, including spectacular oceanfront views and personal concierge service. Head to the oceanfront Infiniti Restaurant & Bar for bites of such fresh local fare as a warm South Caicos lobster salad, garnished with shaved carrots and crispy basil, or the Mahi Mahi carpaccio, with a kick of jalapeño, served to the sound of breaking waves. Looking to stake your umbrella in the sand a little while longer? Rent one of the homes in the Private Villa Collection, a cluster of five freestanding private beachfront residences that come with all the amenities and services of a superior hotel stay, including roundtrip airport transfers, daily housekeeping, and complimentary breakfast.

It has been revealed that A fan-shaped trio of seven-story buildings curve around a beachfront pool and patio at this Grace Bay resort, close to Providenciales's shopping district. Enormous rooms in soft colors have marble baths and soaking tubs, proving that bigger can mean better. Staff members always serve with a smile and make a point of remembering names. The restaurant Seven dishes up Caribbean-inspired cuisine, with entrees like house-made stone crab ravioli, or you can opt for private beachfront dining, complete with a personal butler and a playlist of your choosing. If you're traveling with the family, the kids camp provides diversions such as lizard hunting and sand-castle building—or you can all go for a dip in the island's only heated saltwater pool.

#7201. Even powdery mildew can catch a fungal infection

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (979 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Even powdery mildew can catch a fungal infection

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers found a fungus that infects powdery mildew in preserved specimens, offering clues to how it might help control the crop disease.
  • It has been revealed that powdery mildew is usually the one doing the damage.
  • Researchers checked dried mildew specimens up to about 150 years old and found the parasite on mildews from many countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers found a fungus that infects powdery mildew in preserved specimens, offering clues to how it might help control the crop disease.

It has been revealed that powdery mildew is usually the one doing the damage. The fungi behind it infect crops such as wheat and grapevines, yet some of those mildews are infected themselves, by a fungus called Ampelomyces that lives inside their cells.

Researchers checked dried mildew specimens up to about 150 years old and found the parasite on mildews from many countries.

The study also found that about 13% of the public DNA records labeled Ampelomyces appear to belong to other fungi.

Michael Bradshaw, an assistant professor of entomology and plant pathology at North Carolina State University, led the research with first author Jacklyn Thomas.

Bradshaw directs the university’s Larry F. Grand Mycological Herbarium.

It has been revealed that he sees the parasite as a possible tool against the disease. Part of the reason is host specificity, meaning some strains infect only certain kinds of mildew.

“By understanding hyperparasite diversity and how many different strains are out there, it might give us insights on if some are better at controlling the fungus than others,” Bradshaw said.

“There is a degree of host specificity to these hyperparasites, and if we are able to delve deeper they may be very useful in containing this plant disease.”.

Industry observers note that powdery mildews include more than 900 species. Together they cause disease in more than 10,000 kinds of flowering plants.

Sources indicate that powdery mildew fungi need living plant tissue to grow, so scientists can’t grow them in lab cultures. That makes their parasite hard to study as well.

It has been revealed that so the team turned to herbaria, collections of preserved plants and fungi. The researchers screened 609 mildew specimens held at North Carolina State and at Harvard University’s Farlow Herbarium.

Sources indicate that the specimens came from 28 countries, from Argentina and Morocco to Japan and Ukraine. Many reached North Carolina as gifts from herbaria in Germany and Japan.

From each specimen, the team scraped a bit of mildew and tested its DNA for the parasite.

The researchers then checked every positive result under a microscope.

Researchers lifted the mildew onto clear tape and found Ampelomyces under a microscope.

Sources indicate that ampelomyces turned up in 40 of the 609 specimens, or 6.6%. The authors wrote that old collections let them detect a parasite that is hard to observe directly.

According to recent reports, some kinds of mildew were infected far more often than others. Sawadaea mildews had the highest rate, at 14.3%.

Podosphaera and Phyllactinia mildews were among the lowest, at 3.2% and 2.7%.

Some of those groups had only a few specimens, the authors wrote, so small samples may explain part of the spread.

Researchers in Serbia and Hungary, examining field samples under a microscope, had found the parasite in about a third of them.

The detection rate in the herbarium specimens was much lower.

According to recent reports, the authors suggested reasons for the gap. Their samples came from many parts of the world, and their DNA tests could miss strains whose genetic code differed from what the tests were built to match.

The team sorted its strains, along with hundreds from public records, by how closely related they were.

Strains from Podosphaera mildews tended to group together, and so did strains from a genus called Arthrocladiella.

Strains from Erysiphe, the largest mildew genus, were scattered across many groups.

The mix of tight groups and scattered strains suggests some Ampelomyces lineages specialize while others infect many kinds of mildew.

Several strains from the herbarium specimens matched no known group and may be upcoming lineages.

Sources indicate that one specimen of a mildew called Blumeria showed the parasite under the microscope, but its DNA test failed. The authors suggested that Ampelomyces on Blumeria may be a lineage not yet described.

It has been revealed that genBank is a public database where scientists share DNA sequences. The team downloaded all 671 sequences filed there as Ampelomyces and placed them in one family tree.

Recent findings suggest that of those sequences, 88 fell outside the main Ampelomyces branch. That is how the team arrived at its estimate that about 13% were probably other fungi.

Even samples from culture collections, which supply living strains to labs, were mislabeled.

One strain listed as Ampelomyces had DNA identical to a fungus called Didymella, though the authors wrote that it may have been contaminated after it left the collection.

Bradshaw noted errors like these are a risk whenever researchers rely on large datasets that anyone can add to.

“These parasites are hard to identify, so what happens is someone misidentifies them and enters incorrect data,” he said.

“Then someone else sees that wrong data and uses it to classify their own samples, which leads to more wrong data, and it amplifies that way.”.

Sources indicate that the team’s answer is a checked reference tree of 47 confirmed strains, posted to a free online tool called T-BAS. Researchers can upload a sequence and see where it belongs.

Sources indicate that there are limits. The family tree rests mostly on one short piece of DNA, and its main Ampelomyces branch was only weakly supported.

More genetic data will help sort out how the strains are related, the authors wrote.

Industry observers note that two big questions remain. Are some strains better at fighting the fungus than others?

Sources indicate that and did the parasite and the mildew evolve together? Answering the second question will take more samples and whole genomes.

Future research could also expand sampling to more regions and more mildews.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings B.

How to make friends at freshman orientation

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for new member orientation on Monday.
  • What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?
  • As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for new member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.

Trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s new member orientation. Giddy, even.

Sources indicate that the incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

Recent findings suggest that “I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” said Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

Forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

Industry observers note that “I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he said of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”.

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

In a recent development, “It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” mentioned Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

Recent findings suggest that cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

Sources indicate that “The congressman noted that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s important that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

Sources indicate that “This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke mentioned. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”.

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

Recent findings suggest that “I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” noted Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

But just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” said Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

“I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he mentioned.

Sources indicate that after arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander noted he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he said.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”.

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he remarked.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their upcoming workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” noted Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

“They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander stated.

#7197. Latest Update: The fossil fuel ‘carbon bubble’ may be smaller than investors once feared

Latest Update: The fossil fuel ‘carbon bubble’ may be smaller than investors once feared

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced study estimates a $99.3 billion carbon bubble among major U.S.-listed fossil fuel companies, with climate policy risks varying by firm.
  • Major fossil-fuel companies may be overvalued by about $99.3 billion because of climate policy risks, according to new research.
  • That amounts to roughly 5.5% of the market value examined, suggesting investors have already priced in some of the transition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced study estimates a $99.3 billion carbon bubble among major U.S.-listed fossil fuel companies, with climate policy risks varying by firm.

Major fossil-fuel companies may be overvalued by about $99.3 billion because of climate policy risks, according to new research.

That amounts to roughly 5.5% of the market value examined, suggesting investors have already priced in some of the transition.

Researchers at the University of Technology Sydney’s Centre for Climate Risk and Resilience worked with colleagues at Macquarie University.

They investigated how major climate policy developments affected the value of leading fossil-fuel companies listed in the United States.

In a recent development, the findings suggest a smaller potential correction than some earlier estimates. They also point to considerable differences in how individual companies might fare.

The carbon bubble describes a concern about what fossil-fuel businesses are really worth as the world moves toward cleaner energy.

Their valuations depend partly on future earnings from coal, oil and gas. Stronger climate policies or falling demand could reduce those earnings, leaving reserves undeveloped and infrastructure less valuable.

Industry observers note that if investors underestimate those changes, share prices may be higher than future business prospects justify. A correction could then bring losses for shareholders and financial institutions.

The researchers set out to estimate that gap, while allowing for the possibility that markets already recognize some climate risks.

The team examined 31 major climate policy signals between 1996 and 2023.

These comprised 27 United Nations climate conferences and four significant announcements in the United States and European Union.

Using stock and options market information, they estimated company values under two scenarios.

One assumed business as usual without additional climate-policy constraints; the other incorporated climate-related policy risks.

The difference produced the estimated bubble of 5.5%, or $99.3 billion, for the largest US-listed fossil-fuel companies with traded options.

Recent findings suggest that that figure concerns the companies studied. It does not measure the potential losses across every fossil-fuel business or project worldwide.

Nor does it predict an inevitable crash. The results suggest markets may be adjusting gradually, with some transition risks already reflected in prices.

“The findings challenge the assumption that stronger climate policies must automatically lead to substantial financial losses for every fossil-fuel organization,” mentioned lead researchers Mona Mashhadi Rajabi and Martina Linnenluecke from Sydney.

Recent findings suggest that “Companies are not all equally exposed to the energy transition. Their financial position can depend on the quality of their assets, their investment decisions, their ability to adapt and how effectively they prepare for a changing energy market.”.

“This is an key distinction. A company that recognizes transition risks early, adjusts its investment strategy and prepares for changes in energy demand may be better positioned than one that continues to rely on the assumption that current business conditions will last indefinitely.”.

The sector-wide estimate therefore leaves an crucial question for investors: which businesses are preparing, and which are counting on little changing?

A relatively modest estimate does not remove the uncertainty surrounding future fossil fuel demand.

Projects that look profitable today may earn less under different policies or more competitive clean-energy alternatives.

Assets built to operate for decades are particularly exposed to those changes. Their economics depend on conditions well beyond the next reporting period.

“So, the key message of this research is not that fossil-fuel companies are financially safe. Significant transition risks remain, and these need to be assessed carefully. Importantly, risks will change as the stringency of carbon policies changes,” the scientists explained.

It has been revealed that “For policymakers, the findings reinforce the importance of clear and predictable climate policies. For investors and financial institutions, the results are a reminder to look beyond headline estimates of stranded assets.”.

Sources indicate that stranded assets are reserves or infrastructure that lose economic value before their expected useful life ends. Their potential scale matters, but it cannot alone explain how a whole company will perform.

Sources indicate that investment choices, asset quality, and the ability to change direction also influence future earnings. Assessing those differences requires information about how companies intend to respond.

“Climate-related financial disclosure can help investors distinguish between companies that are preparing for the transition and those that remain heavily exposed to changing market conditions,” the researchers mentioned.

The research puts that distinction at the center of the debate. A single estimate of potential overvaluation cannot tell investors which projects will remain competitive or which strategies will work.

For Australia, the findings have implications beyond the stock market. Decisions about upcoming fossil-fuel projects commit money to assets whose working lives may span substantial changes in overseas demand.

Recent findings suggest that “These questions are particularly crucial for Australia, one of the world’s major exporters of coal and liquefied natural gas (LNG). The value of Australia’s fossil-fuel industries is closely connected to demand in international markets,” the authors wrote.

“Australia therefore needs to look beyond current export revenues when making decisions about future energy investment. A project that appears commercially attractive today may face a different economic outlook over its operating life.”.

“Equally, assuming that all fossil-fuel assets will rapidly lose value could lead to decisions that overlook differences in project economics and market exposure.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The carbon bubble debate should move beyond predictions of a sudden collapse. What matters now is whether companies, investors and governments are making decisions that reflect the energy markets of the future, rather than relying solely on the conditions of the past.”.

The study is published in the journal Sustainable Futures.

#7196. Breaking: Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Breaking: Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.
  • Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

In a recent development, the archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

In a recent development, the distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

According to recent reports, this evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

Industry observers note that the purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

According to recent reports, davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he states. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”.

#7195. A vanished bird from Haiti may help solve an ancient Pacific mystery

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1360 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

A vanished bird from Haiti may help solve an ancient Pacific mystery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DNA reveals how snipes and woodcocks reached distant islands, stopped migrating, changed physically, and became vulnerable to extinction.
  • The sandpiper family includes some of the most extreme long-distance migrants among birds.
  • Industry observers note that two branches of that family, the snipes and the woodcocks, have behaved quite differently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DNA reveals how snipes and woodcocks reached distant islands, stopped migrating, changed physically, and became vulnerable to extinction.

The sandpiper family includes some of the most extreme long-distance migrants among birds.

Industry observers note that two branches of that family, the snipes and the woodcocks, have behaved quite differently. These birds reached islands again and again, and migration was then abandoned.

Nearly every living species was examined in a new DNA study.

In a recent development, the results suggest that island settlement was accompanied by changes in body size and flying ability. Island species later proved vulnerable when people arrived with rats and cats.

The work was led by Min Zhao, then a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. Colleagues at Virginia Tech and the Field Museum in Chicago also took part.

Recent findings suggest that according to Zhao, the whole project grew out of one extinct bird from Hispaniola. That Caribbean island is shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic.

The dates reported in the study were estimated from family trees built with DNA. The uncertainty attached to them can run to millions of years.

Florida Museum researchers dug the bird’s bones out of a cave in Haiti in 1984.

In 2015, those bones were described by two scientists as a fresh species of woodcock. Woodcocks are long-billed birds that probe soft soil for food.

It has been revealed that one of the two scientists was David Steadman, who is now an emeritus curator at the museum. He is also listed as a co-author of the newly introduced study.

In a recent development, zhao’s team extracted DNA from two of the fossil specimens. The researchers then read the mitochondrial genome, a small set of genes passed from mother to offspring.

According to recent reports, both specimens were placed with the snipes, which form the sister group of the woodcocks. Their closest living relative turned out to be the giant snipe of lowland South America.

In a recent development, the analysis suggested a South American origin for the Haitian bird’s ancestors. The two lineages are thought to have split between 5 and 12 million years ago.

Industry observers note that why, then, did the bones resemble those of a woodcock? The authors think the bird’s build may have been altered by island living, which could explain the mix-up.

The outer wing bone of the Haitian bird was unusually short when compared with its upper wing bone. The authors wrote that it could fly but probably not well.

According to recent reports, the team sequenced 45 samples in total. Two were the Haitian fossils and 19 were toe pads taken from old museum specimens. The remaining 24 were fresh tissue samples.

All but one of the 29 living species of snipes and woodcocks were covered by these samples. Specimens were supplied by ten museums and research collections.

A family tree was built from the data, and both groups were traced back to Eurasia.

The ancestors of today’s American birds crossed from the Eastern Hemisphere to the Western Hemisphere four separate times.

One of those crossings took place roughly 20 million years ago. It was then that the ancestor of the American woodcock reached North America.

The researchers could not tell whether the bird arrived across the Atlantic or by way of Alaska.

It has been revealed that the Austral snipes are found on the outlying islands of New Zealand. Scientists have long placed these small brown birds in a group of their own.

Some snipes from Eurasia spend each winter in Australia and on nearby islands. The DNA revealed that those visitors are not close relatives of the Austral snipes.

Instead, the Austral snipes share a branch with several large South American snipes and the extinct Haitian bird.

Two DNA datasets placed the split between the Austral snipes and their relatives at about 14 million and nearly 18 million years ago, respectively.

The southern continents had broken apart long before either estimate. The snipes’ ancestor most likely crossed the Pacific.

According to recent reports, how the crossing happened remains an open question. The authors suggested that birds straying far outside their normal range may have played a role. Such straying was perhaps caused by extreme weather.

According to recent reports, the authors also raised a route through Antarctica. Patches of treeless tundra are thought to have lasted there until at least 12.8 million years ago.

Several living snipe species still breed on tundra in the Arctic.

The analysis indicated that the ancestors of both snipes and woodcocks were migrants. Their island descendants are not.

Ten of the 29 living species are found only on islands, and none of those ten migrates.

In a recent development, the habit was lost several times. Woodcocks gave it up when they settled the Malay Archipelago in Southeast Asia. Snipes did the same when they settled South America and Madagascar.

Body size changed as well, although not in a single direction.

The Amami woodcock of southern Japan is about 45% heavier than the Eurasian woodcock, its closest mainland relative. Madagascar’s snipe is about 91% heavier than the common snipe of Eurasia.

Industry observers note that the opposite change is seen in the Austral snipes. Their average weight is 3.4 ounces (96 grams), which is about the weight of a deck of cards.

Sources indicate that south American snipes on the same branch average 8.6 ounces (243.5 grams). That is more than twice as much.

The smaller size may be explained by scarce food, the authors suggested. Competition from kiwis and other birds that probe the soil for worms was also considered possible.

According to recent reports, ten species of snipes and woodcocks are known to have died out in the recent geologic past. Nine of them lived on islands.

According to recent reports, the Austral snipes suffered the heaviest losses. Three of nine known species survive. All three are ranked as Vulnerable or Near Threatened by the IUCN Red List.

The South Island snipe died out in 1964, and introduced black rats are regarded as the likely cause.

Recent findings suggest that no resident snipe or woodcock is left in the Caribbean. At least three species have been lost there.

The youngest dated bones of the Haitian bird are about 600 years old. Rats and feral cats brought by people are suspected of causing its extinction.

Recent findings suggest that snipes nest on the ground, where they can be reached by those predators. Island species had given up migration, and in some cases strong flight as well.

The authors wrote that these changes made such species especially vulnerable to human impacts.

Overhunting was named as one of those impacts.

Jessica Oswald, a co-author, also worked on the study at the Florida Museum.

In a recent development, “People will eat anything,” noted Oswald. She said a crew of hungry explorers or whalers could wipe out an island’s birds in a single weekend.

According to recent reports, island woodcocks in Japan and Southeast Asia appear to have fared better. They live in mountain forests, which may be harder for people to reach.

Upcoming Zealand may have been reached first by the Austral snipes.

From there they could have spread to Norfolk Island, New Caledonia and Fiji. The opposite path cannot be ruled out, because no genetic data exist for those islands’ extinct snipes.

More snipe species may once have lived in the Pacific and are now extinct. In that case, today’s birds would be the last survivors of a larger group. Direct fossil evidence of that link across the Pacific is still missing.

Industry observers note that the Haitian bird’s place on the tree rests on mitochondrial genes from two specimens. A possible close relative from Puerto Rico is also extinct and has not been tested genetically.

The authors suggest that DNA from fossils yet to be found on Pacific islands could help trace how snipes spread across the region.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

At Our Annual Points of View Summit, Experts Make Their 2027 Travel Predictions

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world.
  • Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.
  • Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of massive-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world. Spliced between compelling panels on Lowcountry heritage, summer travel trends, and the evolving appeal of all-inclusive stays, the breakouts allowed for extended discussions with Traveler editors on a range of themes. From culinary experiences inspired by Hilton Head Island's Gullah cuisine, to the evolving dynamics of multigenerational travel and a newly introduced guard of ultra-luxe globetrotters, we got the inside scoop on where travelers are going and how they're getting there.

Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.

Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of massive-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.

According to recent reports, our specialists all agreed that travelers yearn for “authentic” food moments, though defining authenticity—and actually finding it—often becomes tricky. To Omolola Campbell, sixth-gen Gullah descendant and executive producer of Gullah short documentary The Spirit We Move With, it's about who provides the experience. “Taking a cooking class is much different than getting it from a local chef who can tell stories about why a dish means so much to this locality,” she said, explaining how so many of South Carolina's Gullah dishes contain okra because its seeds were sown into the hair of West Africans who were brought to the South for slavery. The plant has come to represent resilience, and it's that integral context, according to her, that gives a meal its soul. “That's how you differentiate the person who really knows why they're cooking what they're cooking,” Campbell concluded.

Dana Kravis, Madison Flager, and our travel specialists explore multigenerational travel trends.

Sources indicate that when it comes to multigenerational trips, the grandchildren are choosing the destinations and the grandparents are paying—it's their way of leaving a legacy amongst those dearest to them. During a discussion led by global executive director of video Dana Kravis and commerce director Madison Flager, our travel specialists observed that, because people today tend to wait longer to have children, grandparents are older than they used to be. Travelers in their 80s and 90s are increasingly joining trips, shifting the multigenerational travel dynamic away from the traditional picture of grandparents in their 70s. To trip designers, this means there must be layers of options catering to different activity and exertion levels.

Sources indicate that many in this session agreed the most successful family trips provide opportunities for separating and coming back together. Three itinerary choices in one day are ideal, so younger folks can be out and about, with the whole family reuniting for mealtimes and perhaps an afternoon activity. Boat and yacht experiences were especially recommended as spaces where the family is forced to be together—grandkids cannot simply run off and do their own thing.

Industry observers note that what's luxury to one traveler might seem the furthest from it to another; some long for jam-packed, once-in-a-lifetime itineraries, while others want total disconnection and the privilege to do absolutely nothing for a week. Features director Rebecca Misner and commerce writer Jessica Sulima led this breakout, as specialists debated the definition of luxury itself. “Luxury is being able to pass on meaning to kids [and] exposing families to the broader world and its cultures,” Virgi Schiffino Kennedy, managing partner at Lux Voyage, mentioned of its intangible appeal. To Ruchi Harnal, founder of Harnal Travel, true luxury “is not about the resort or the villa but the personalization of the trip.” As for who’s spending money on trips? Thomas Robinson, MR at Dehouche, has observed that Gen Z and Millennials are more inclined to spend but want to know where that money goes. Additionally, the specialists largely agreed they’re seeing a shift away from parents taking their children on trips, and towards 30- and 40-somethings treating their parents to a vacation. In Harnal's experience, milestone birthdays and anniversaries are driving clients to book a trip.

Between rising temperatures and overtourism, our specialists discuss the factors impacting European summer destinations.

What is the impact of overtourism, price inflation, and rising temperatures on our Euro summers? Director of special projects Lale Arikoglu and commerce editor Meaghan Kenny opened the floor for our specialists. “If you’re thinking of traveling to the Dolomites, consider Switzerland instead. There’s history and beautiful scenery with fewer crowds,” Brian Dore, owner of CIU Travel, said. For the hiking curious, some added that Switzerland offers plenty of one-day hiking trails or “soft adventure” travel—three-to-four days combined with a lake or city destination. Others agreed that traveling to the Alps offers a significant advantage—higher elevations means cooler temperatures—and that Slovenia is a great alternative to Italy. To dodge the crowds, travelers might also consider Belgium, Denmark, or Norway (where ocean ships and river cruises are opening earlier in March). For families, consider Umbria (hot tip: plenty of festival and craft opportunities for kids), Austria, Ireland, or Croatia.

In a recent development, for those who want to stick with more tried-and-tested European itineraries next summer, consider going as early as possible, for instance, in May instead of August. When it comes to traveling to France specifically, folks advised flying into Paris or Nice, then venturing out to the countryside or oft-overlooked Atlantic Coast. And our specialists could not stress it enough: Always, always check the temperatures in advance of your trip.

As discussed by Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina, during the panel on summer travel, the demand for travel to Asia is only increasing. Global features director Erin Florio and editorial assistant Kat Chen continued the conversation with travel specialists on the destinations and experiences driving this growth. For Silk Road Treasure Tours president Zulya Rajabova and her clients, it's the destinations with indispensable craft identities, such as Samarkand in Uzbekistan with its millennia-old design traditions, that make the continent so varied yet distinct. Meanwhile, Marigold Wood, travel designer at Blonde Atlas, explained that she's been recommending routes going through China, such as Yunnan's tea trails, which offer trekking and hiking opportunities. For Ethan Crowley, lead trip designer at Asia Desk Ltd, educating his travelers on navigating countries like Cambodia, beyond their most-visited landmarks, is key.

According to recent reports, if 2026 was the year of the fan, 2027 is ushering in even more reasons to travel for entertainment. Associate editor Charlie Hobbs and commerce writer Jessica Chapel helmed this breakout on the sporting events, music festivals, and art fairs that specialists are seeing people travel for (and the subsequent hurdles they must overcome to). From Pink at the Sphere, where access requires a Venetian hotel package to the Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, where full-house and package buyouts, high-demand events are increasingly forcing bundled purchases.

Sources indicate that the specialists also highlighted how limited legal protections in the States enables extreme ticket scalping for stadium concerts and makes domestic events increasingly unaffordable. Stephanie Malakie, founder of Empress Travel Club pointed to a related challenge: With so many events and providers, travel advisors find it hard to filter the options and identify the right fit for clients. Rather than just acquiring a ticket, specialists agreed the focus should be on curating the surrounding experience or tapping into evergreen and niche experiential travel, with events like the Jets playing in London or F1 in Shanghai. Cultural milestones like Vatican City trips featuring Papal Blessings or European Christmas markets pair well with entertainment, too. To Zhang, set-jetting to filming locations also offers value, minus the headache of peak-event ticketing.

Hannah Towey co-leads the breakout session on outdoor travel.

Everyone is hiking, or so it seems. Helmed by Jamie Spain, travel bookings commerce editor, and Hannah Towey, news editor, this breakout explored nature as wellness and why it is we're increasingly longing for all things outdoorsy. However, our specialists offered a frank reality check on our dumbphone fantasies. “Guests all want to have access [to Wi-Fi] for emergency reasons at a minimum… I don’t have a single guest who wants to [fully] digital detox," Kate Doty, trip designer at Geographic Expeditions, stated. It seems that many travelers want to be disconnected until the time comes for true disconnection, and Lou Lagrange, trip consultant at Luxury Travel Advisor, added, “Even planning for national park trips, [you have to] warn them there won’t be Wi-Fi.” However, the group observed that services such as having photographers on small ships, helps reduce a traveler's dependency on their phones.

In a recent development, there's still a real demand for glamping, as guests want access to nature but with a side of luxury. And when it comes to extreme weather events, instead of having travelers write off entire regions or countries, Doty has figured out collaborative ways to shelve them for potential future trips. In Travel Studio founder Kerri Lisa's case, it's a matter of reframing the perks of a destination and its seasons; the rainy season, for example, might be exceptionally lush and green. There's always something to be learned in welcoming a bit of playful unpredictability into our itineraries.
