Wind turbines may have killed nearly 19 million bats in the U.S. since 1981

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study draws on decades of wind farm surveys to estimate how many bats turbines killed across the lower 48 states from 1981 to 2024.
  • The bats that die under wind turbines are picked up one carcass at a time, by crews walking the ground under each tower.
  • For decades, those site-by-site counts were the main tally anyone had.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study draws on decades of wind farm surveys to estimate how many bats turbines killed across the lower 48 states from 1981 to 2024.

The bats that die under wind turbines are picked up one carcass at a time, by crews walking the ground under each tower.

For decades, those site-by-site counts were the main tally anyone had.

Combining those counts with a statistical model, researchers estimated that wind turbines killed about 18.7 million bats in the lower 48 states from 1981 through the end of the study period.

Industry observers note that since 2021, the toll has run above 1.5 million a year. That is a scale the authors wrote may rival the fungal disease that has devastated cave-hibernating bats.

Charles Labuzzetta of the U.S. Geological Survey‘s Fort Collins Science Center led the analysis with colleagues at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Laboratory of the Rockies.

The figures are model estimates with wide ranges, built from monitoring that was never designed to be added up, and the relationships they found are correlations, not proven causes.

In an interview with Earth.com, Labuzzetta noted the data behind the study were richer than their patchy origins suggest.

“We found that there could still be a lot to learn from the rich monitoring data that has been collected since the late 1990s and continues to be collected,” he noted.

The team pulled together 499 monitoring reports from 277 wind facilities in the lower 48 states, filed with the Fish and Wildlife Service since the late 1990s.

Each report counted the carcasses found under turbines and estimated how many were missed. But the searches differed in length, area and method, and many reports are confidential.

A statistical model pooled them, corrected for what the searchers could not see, and projected fatalities back to 1981.

The median came out at 18,696,140 bats across ten species, with a plausible range of about 13.3 million to 25.7 million.

That is the estimate for the lower 48 states that the compliance reports could never produce on their own.

Four species account for nearly all of it. The authors estimate about 6.7 million hoary bats, 5.8 million eastern red bats, 3.4 million silver-haired bats and 1.5 million substantial brown bats.

Recent findings suggest that on average, a turbine killed close to six hoary bats a year. At the other end, the rare Indiana bat accounted for about 6,000 deaths over the whole period.

The last national figures date from 2013, and they put the toll in the hundreds of thousands a year.

Those estimates leaned on a single rule of thumb, about 1.7 hoary bats per megawatt of capacity.

According to recent reports, A projection built on it assumed roughly 113,000 hoary bat deaths in 2012, and the fresh model estimates about 268,000 for that year. The old figure was less than half the new one.

The gap matters because of what the old projection, built on expert judgment, already said.

In a recent development, run on the lower numbers, it warned that hoary bats could lose 50% to 90% of their population within 50 years. Eastern red bats have been dying faster still, more than 500,000 a year since 2021.

Rated capacity, the usual yardstick, turned out to be a poor predictor of deaths. The area swept by the blades was a better predictor.

On most turbines built since 2020 that is 2.5 to 5 acres (10,000 to 20,000 square meters).

Researchers estimated more deaths among several bat species at turbines whose blades swept a larger area or passed closer to the ground.

Industry observers note that for all ten species, estimated deaths were higher at wind farms closer to rivers. The study couldn’t determine whether being near a river was itself responsible for the higher toll.

Labuzzetta told Earth.com those patterns point to siting and design as levers, but not to a single fix.

“There is still a great deal to learn about what strategies may be optimal and could provide the greatest conservation management return on investment for individual species and across all species,” he said.

White-nose syndrome, a fungal disease first seen in 2006, has cut some cave-hibernating species by more than 90%.

The authors compared their total with one rough estimate of the disease’s losses and found the two comparable in size.

The two threats mostly hit different bats. The disease kills bats that hibernate in caves, while turbines mostly kill the migratory tree-roosting species.

Across North American bats as a whole, the authors wrote, the two may compound.

Whether 18.7 million deaths translate into shrinking populations is the question the study can’t answer.

Sources indicate that data on how many hoary or eastern red bats exist, how long they live and how fast they breed are largely unavailable, the authors wrote. So the same number of deaths could mean a crisis or a dent.

“Our research alone cannot answer whether fatalities from wind energy are leading to similar population-level declines for migratory tree-roosting bat species,” Labuzzetta mentioned.

Population trends from the North American Bat Monitoring Program could begin to fill that gap.

The authors also called for monitoring at wind farms to be collected and shared in a form that can be pooled.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The 8 Best MagSafe-Compatible Portable Chargers For On-the-Go Charging

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • A good portable battery pack keeps your phone alive through long travel days, packed schedules, and everything in between.
  • The first MagSafe batteries charged at a sluggish 5 watts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A good portable battery pack keeps your phone alive through long travel days, packed schedules, and everything in between. If you have a MagSafe iPhone (the iPhone 12 or newer) or an Android phone that supports Qi2, a magnetic pack is the most convenient choice: it clicks onto the back of our favorite phones and starts charging, with no cable to carry.

These packs have come a long way. The first MagSafe batteries charged at a sluggish 5 watts. Many of today’s Qi2 packs deliver 15 watts, and the newest Qi2.2 models reach 25 watts while fitting twice the battery into a body about as thin as your phone. Plenty also add built-in cables, kickstands, and fast USB-C ports for topping up a second device.

Sources indicate that all that progress means more choice, and more spec sheets that look the same. We’ve rounded up the best MagSafe portable chargers you can buy right now, from slim everyday packs to fast premium picks, so you can find the right one for you.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve used MagSafe battery packs with my iPhone for years. The ones I kept using had a strong magnet and enough battery to get through a day away from an outlet. Most picks here support Qi2, which charges at 15 watts, or Qi2.2, which charges at up to 25 watts on an iPhone 16 or newer. I looked for packs around 10,000 mAh, since that size can charge most phones and then some. I also looked for a USB-C port of 30 watts or more, so the pack itself recharges quickly.

Sources indicate that the INIU SnapGo Air packs a 10,000 mAh battery into a body just half an inch thick. It supports Qi2.2 wireless charging at up to 25 watts, and INIU states it can take an iPhone 17 Pro from empty to 50 percent in 33 minutes. That top speed works on the iPhone 16 Plus, 16 Pro Max, and newer models running iOS 26. The iPhone 12 through 15 charge at 15 watts.

Industry observers note that for faster charging, plug in the USB-C cable attached to the pack. It delivers 45 watts, which INIU claims charges an iPhone 17 Pro from 20 to 78 percent in 25 minutes. The pack also supports passthrough charging, so when it’s plugged into the wall, it charges itself and your phone at the same time. The cable doubles as a lanyard and detaches, and a digital display highlights the exact battery percentage.

According to recent reports, for $23, the LISEN Ultra Slim charges at the same 15-watt Qi2 speed as the Anker Nano, which costs more than twice as much. It’s 0.38 inches thick and weighs 3.6 ounces. LISEN claims it charges an iPhone 17 to about 50 percent in an hour. Past 75 percent, it slows down on purpose to protect your phone’s battery.

According to recent reports, LISEN lists the battery as 5,000 mAh but gives a rated capacity of 3,000 mAh. The rated number is closer to how much charge reaches your phone, so plan on a partial top-up rather than a full charge. Plugged in with a USB-C cable, it charges at up to 20 watts. It only works with the iPhone 12 through 18. LISEN recommends pairing it with a MagSafe case, since other cases can cause overheating.

Sources indicate that the Anker MagGo 2 Pro costs twice as much as our top pick, and most of that extra money goes toward cooling. Wireless charging creates heat, and many packs slow down as they warm up. This one has a small fan and layers of graphene that Anker says keep it cool, so it can stay at its top speed of 25 watts for longer. It’s rated to charge an iPhone 18 Pro to 50 percent in 25 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that its USB-C port runs at 45 watts in both directions, fast enough to refill the pack from 0 to 80 percent in under an hour. A screen shows battery level, charging speed, temperature, and battery health, and a built-in stand folds out to prop up your phone for video.

UGREEN says the MagFlow can fully charge an iPhone 17 Pro Max more than 2.5 times before it needs a wall outlet. At 20,000 mAh, it holds twice as much as our top pick, and a digital display on the side highlights how much is left.

Recent findings suggest that wireless charging runs at up to 25 watts, which UGREEN says gets an iPhone 18 Pro to 50 percent in 30 minutes. The built-in USB-C cable on the side doubles as a carry strap, and UGREEN rates it for more than 10,000 bends. The pack's USB-C port charges at up to 45 watts and refills the pack at the same rate, and a USB-A port lets you plug in older cables.

Fitting twice the battery makes the MagFlow heavier and thicker than our 10,000 mAh picks. That makes it harder to slip into a pocket, and it adds noticeable weight to the back of your phone while it charges.

It has been revealed that the Sharge Icemag 3 has a see-through case that shows the internal components, plus a subtle RGB light. It charges wirelessly at up to 25 watts using Qi2.2, and Sharge states that gets an iPhone 17 Pro from zero to 50 percent in 30 minutes. A built-in fan keeps the pack’s surface cool, so charging stays steady. The fan doesn't lower your phone's temperature.

Recent findings suggest that A fold-out kickstand holds your phone upright or sideways for video calls. The built-in USB-C cable and a second USB-C port sit on the side, so you can still hold your phone normally while it charges via cable. Unlike the previous two picks, the wired connection charges a bit slower at up to 35 watts.

It has been revealed that the Anker Nano Magnetic Power Bank is 0.34 inches thick and weighs 4.3 ounces, about a third less than the INIU. Because it’s Qi2 rather than Qi2.2, it charges wirelessly at up to 15 watts. Its 5,000 mAh battery is half the size of our other picks, but that makes it more pocketable.

It has been revealed that anker’s own figures show it charging an iPhone 17 to 85 percent and an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 63 percent with the phone in Low Power Mode. That makes it a backup for a long day, not a full refill. A graphene layer inside spreads heat, so the pack stays cool. The USB-C port charges a phone at up to 20 watts, and the pack comes in six colors with a two-year warranty.

In a recent development, if you take your phone on hikes or to the beach, the TORRAS MiniMag Pro is the magnetic pack to get. TORRAS rates it IP54, so it should be protected from dust and splashes from any direction; however, it isn't meant for underwater use.

Inside is a semi-solid-state battery that TORRAS claims passed puncture, crush, and drop testing. An aluminum frame wraps the body, and a digital display demonstrates the remaining charge.

Wireless charging tops out at 15 watts, and with a USB-C cable, the pack charges a phone at up to 30 watts. With passthrough charging, one cable plugged into the wall charges the pack and your phone together overnight.

In a recent development, the iPhone Air gave up battery capacity to get its thin body, and Apple’s answer is a battery pack built just for it. On the Air, Apple says it adds up to 65 percent more charge. The pack is shaped around the Air's camera bump, so it doesn't fit other iPhones.

Sources indicate that while it fits the Air perfectly, wireless charging tops out at 12 watts. For faster top-ups, leave the battery attached and plug your phone into a 25-watt or higher adapter; the phone and battery charge together. The pack also has no battery readout. Instead, a single hidden light glows green while it charges and orange when it runs low.

Check the box for Qi2 or Qi2.2. Qi2 packs charge wirelessly at up to 15 watts, while Qi2.2 packs reach 25 watts, which Apple notes can bring an iPhone 17 Pro to 50 percent in about 30 minutes. Packs sold as "magnetic" or "MagSafe-compatible" without Qi2 certification often charge at just 7.5 watts.

The iPhone 12 through 15 charge at 15 watts even on a Qi2.2 pack, so if you own one, a cheaper Qi2 pack will charge it just as fast. For 25 watts, you need a newer phone, such as the iPhone 16 series and later models running iOS 26.

For most people, I recommend a pack around 10,000 mAh, the size of our top pick. Don't expect two full charges, though. Some power is lost in the battery cells and in the circuits that convert it for your phone. Anker indicates its 10,000 mAh pack delivers about 5,500 to 6,500 mAh to your phone. A 5,000 mAh pack is thinner and lighter, but it works best as a midday top-up. A 20,000 mAh pack can recharge a phone several times, but the extra weight and thickness make it harder to carry.

In a recent development, every magnetic pack has a USB-C port, which refills the pack and can charge a second device. Look for one rated at 30 watts or higher. At 45 watts, a pack can fast-charge a phone over a cable and refill itself quickly. Anker says the MagGo 2 Pro reaches 80 percent in 52 minutes. If you want to charge the pack and your phone overnight from one outlet, look for passthrough charging.

Recent findings suggest that faster wireless charging produces more heat, and many packs cut their charging speed as they warm up. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro and Sharge Icemag 3 use small fans to maintain speed. Thick cases trap heat too. Anker recommends a case no thicker than 2.4 mm.

It has been revealed that most magnetic packs are designed around iPhones. Anker and LISEN don't recommend their packs for Android phones, and Apple’s own battery fits only the iPhone Air. If you use a case, make sure it's MagSafe-compatible, or the magnet won't hold well.

#7170. Industry News: A giant planet stopped crossing its star while astronomers watched, and it never left

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1139 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A giant planet stopped crossing its star while astronomers watched, and it never left

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers saw a planet around a single star stop crossing it, a first.
  • It has been revealed that astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years.
  • The planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers saw a planet around a single star stop crossing it, a first. A hidden neighbor is likely tipping its orbit.

It has been revealed that astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years. Then, in March 2026, it stopped showing up.

The planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere. Its orbit has tipped, most likely from the pull of a second planet in the same system, one that astronomers haven’t detected directly.

TOI-2535 b, more than 1,000 light-years away, is the first confirmed planet around a single star that astronomers have seen stop crossing. Samuel Yee, a 51 Pegasi b Postdoctoral Fellow at UCLA, led the work with UCLA astrophysicist Erik Petigura.

Sources indicate that each of those crossings is called a transit. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so rapidly that its transit disappeared while we were watching,” Yee said.

When a planet passes between its star and Earth, it blocks a little of the starlight. The star dims for a few hours, and that small dip is how NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) finds newly introduced worlds.

Sources indicate that A transit only shows up if the star, the planet and Earth line up almost perfectly. If the orbit tips by just a few degrees, the planet passes above or below the star as seen from Earth, and the star never dims.

TESS checked on the star, called TOI-2535, five times between April 2019 and March 2026.

The planet orbiting it is a hot Jupiter, a gas giant that orbits very close to its star. It goes around once every 8.24 days. Mercury takes 88 days, more than 10 times as long.

It has been revealed that to confirm the planet, the team used an instrument on the 11.5-foot (3.5-meter) WIYN telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona. It tracked how the star shifted back and forth, and the measurements ruled out a small star.

Most planets that cross their stars keep a steady schedule. TOI-2535 b’s crossings came as much as six hours early or late. No hot Jupiter that circles its star in under 10 days has a bigger timing swing on record.

Each crossing was also a little shorter than the last, and each one dimmed the star a little less.

A planet blocks less light, for less time, as its path moves from the middle of a star toward its edge.

It has been revealed that over seven years, the path likely moved across more than half of the star’s face. It passed the middle, grazed the edge, then missed the star entirely.

From the ground, the team tried 15 times and caught a crossing only six times, because the planet kept arriving when it wasn’t expected.

When TESS looked again in March 2026, it found no crossing anywhere in the window where the planet could have shown up.

It has been revealed that so what’s pulling on it? Planets in the same system tug on each other. If two orbits are tilted relative to one another, those tugs slowly swing the direction each orbit faces.

According to recent reports, the team’s computer models suggest the neighbor is at least as massive as Saturn, so it’s probably a second giant planet. The two likely move in a simple rhythm, such as one circling twice for every lap of the other.

By the models, the two orbits must be tilted at least 5 degrees apart to turn this fast.

In a recent development, in most tightly packed systems, orbits stay within 1 to 2 degrees of each other. If this tilt holds up, the system will be one of only a handful so far out of line.

“We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true. If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits,” Yee noted.

“We know of a few systems that are like this. This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly.”.

Petigura used Earth’s moon to explain it.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura noted.

In a recent development, “But because the moon’s orbit is tilted, eclipses are less common. The tilt of the moon’s orbit is a relic of its violent formation history, which resulted from a collision with the early Earth.”.

The same geometry decides when TOI-2535 b will be back. The team calculated that each orbit goes through a full cycle every 30 to 50 years.

The researchers expect the planet to start crossing its star again within that span. Its hidden neighbor could start crossing even sooner.

Early planet formation models suggested giant planets need lots of ice to form. So hot Jupiters probably formed far from their stars and moved closer later.

How? Yee and Petigura see two ways. One is violent. A near-collision knocks the planet onto a stretched-out orbit, and the star pulls it in.

The other is slow. The planet drifts inward with other planets through the gas and dust around a young star. This way should leave the orbits flat.

TOI-2535 b has a close giant neighbor, so it couldn’t have come the violent way, the team wrote.

Sources indicate that “Because TOI-2535 b has a close neighbor, it probably migrated by slowly spiraling in instead of getting flung in,” Yee said. “We may be seeing a formation channel that doesn’t happen very often but is very interesting.”.

It has been revealed that the tilt is still a loose end. The researchers think parts of the system may have tugged on each other later, tipping the orbits over time.

Sources indicate that hundreds of hot Jupiters are known around other stars. Few have a planet close enough to change their orbits. When one does, the neighbor is almost always much smaller. The only other known exception is WASP-148.

Industry observers note that the team can’t say how massive the neighbor is or where it orbits. The crossing times also scattered more than the models predicted.

The star’s back-and-forth motion was jumpier than expected for an old, calm star, too. Both clues could mean there’s more than one unseen planet.

TESS’s first four years of data alone couldn’t have clearly shown the shrinking crossings.

With no crossings left to time, the researchers wrote that the best way forward is to measure the star’s back-and-forth motion often. A neighbor as heavy as the models suggest should show up in that data on its own.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The 40 Best Resorts in Mexico: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world.
  • View all of the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here.
  • The most distinctive part of Hilton’s luxury debut on Mexico’s Riviera Maya is its chameleon-like approach to hospitality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year, our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in Upcoming York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or a TK centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best resorts in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here.

The most distinctive part of Hilton’s luxury debut on Mexico’s Riviera Maya is its chameleon-like approach to hospitality. Yes, with its 349 rooms, acres of pools, 11 restaurants, and kids’ and teens’ clubs, the Conrad is the type of resort whose (large bronze) gates a traveler would be content to pass through only twice: right before check-in and right after checkout. Spiritually, though, it aligns more closely with the smaller-scale properties 30 minutes north in Tulum that seek to connect guests with the surrounding destination. Honoring the Mayan cultures that have occupied this stretch of Caribbean coast for centuries, a traditional sacbe, or “white road”—the name of the ancient roadways Mayans created to travel by moonlight—cuts through the jungled grounds. In the lobby, a soaring art installation takes a cue from Mayan macramé. And at the cenote-inspired spa, a traditional four-hands massage is second only to a jalapeño margarita in the open-air bar as a way to immediately shed any lingering real-life stress remaining after a dip in the sea.

Sources indicate that beaches with sand as soft as silk and water as pure as a turquoise gem sound like a dream, and the balmy surroundings of the Hyatt Zilara Riviera Maya make that vision a reality. An adult-only resort just a 30-minute drive away from Cancun International Airport (CUN), this Hyatt outpost makes booking in some much-needed R&R more convenient than ever. The beach is truly at your fingertips at this reader-favorite hideaway with swim-up suites, bars right on the shore, and the Zen Spa which perches right above it all. You may be parked at this bolthole in the Caribbean, but when it comes to your dining options, the world comes to you. The property houses seven bars and restaurants that cater to every palette, whether you're looking for coastal Italian one night or sushi the next.

Along a palm-studded stretch of coast in the Yucatán Peninsula is the recently opened SLS Playa Mujeres, a 498-room resort offering an array of suites, some with a private balcony, terrace, or a garden with a swim-out pool. The opening of SLS Playa Mujeres also marks the debut of SLS Elite, a selection of rooms offering benefits, including private lounge access, preferred dining reservations, and entry to an exclusive beach. Available to all guests on an all-inclusive basis are 18 restaurant and bar concepts, including Mediterranean-inspired dining at Fi’lia and Cleo, fresh catch at Caracol, and classic steakhouse fare at Union. At the heart of the resort is the 20,000-square-foot Ciel Spa, a wellness destination with thermal baths and an outdoor tranquility pool.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Here, the first cocktail arrives before you do, served aboard the open-bar catamaran that carries you from Cancún to this adult-only retreat on Isla Mujeres. Joining Hyatt’s Unbound Collection in November 2026, Impression lives up to its name, with terraces cascading toward a sheltered beach and rooftop infinity pools that give you every reason to admire the water without venturing down to it. Each of the 125 suites comes with dedicated butler service and all-inclusive coverage, including gourmet à la carte dining. At Spezia, decadent Italian cooking offers a reason to dress for dinner, though your butler can arrange a quieter evening in, should you desire.

Opened in February 2022, this Costa Mujeres gem has become a winner for its stand-out dining (including a food truck and on-site Japanese restaurant) as well as a beachfront pool deck complete with a glass-sided infinity pool. The modern amenities and standout service make it clear this is a five-star property, and guests love the poolside sushi and steak as much as the vast beachfront and unending views.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Industry observers note that etéreo, Auberge Collection is only a 30-minute drive from the Cancún airport, but this slice of heaven on the Riviera Maya feels light-years away from the chaos. The resort is incredibly family-friendly, but not in a way that sacrifices any of its sophistication. It’s the type of place where you stay put and enjoy everything it has to offer, like luxurious spa treatments, unique culinary experiences, and pool and beachside lounging, unless you’re going on one of the excursions organized by the hotel, which range from water activities, like cenote exploration and sailing to a tour of the local archaeological zones. Every single one of the 75 rooms is ocean-facing, with floor to ceiling sliding glass doors framing the view, and leading to private terraces perched above the mangroves. Couples and families with young kids looking for an easy, peaceful escape would do well to book a stay at this intimate property.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Staying at the Viceroy Riviera Maya is a vacation in the truest sense of the word: Palapa villas with lots of wood and rattan (many with private pools and outdoor showers) are connected by meandering pathways that fan out to lush, fragrant gardens. And it’s all fronted by seven miles of glorious, white sand beaches. Just remember that you are in the jungle, so be sure to keep your eye out for wily spider monkeys.

This palm-studded resort has been one of the most beloved destinations on the Riviera Maya since it opened in 1995. But a complete reimagining of the 72-room hotel has given it a renewed edge over its neighbors—without losing any of its soul. Arriving at Maroma involves driving through thick mangroves where spider monkeys swing from the trees (the property sits on 200 acres of jungle) before reaching its signature whitewashed architecture and thatched roofs. The design still leans heavily on the region’s Mayan vernacular—the curved stucco buildings are based on ancient geometric principles—and wider Mexican craftsmanship. In fact, almost every detail of the restoration, overseen by interior designer Tara Bernerd, prioritized Mexican makers and artisans (80 percent of the property’s furnishings and objects were made in the country), from the hand-painted Saltillo floor tiles and woven wall hangings to the cotton “manta” caftans left in rooms for guests to slip into. Rooms overlook the palm tree-lined pool, the Caribbean Sea, or both, and feature more of those beautiful tiles, along with whitewashed walls hung with regional textiles. Every detail is designed to keep guests rooted in the Yucatán Peninsula: Even the in-room bar, which is far from mini, is stocked with local spirits like pox, a Mayan liquor made of corn, sugarcane, and wheat, and Mayalen Guerrero mezcal in a beau­tiful bottle. Of the two restaurants on site, the pick is Casa Mayor from Mexican chef Daniel Camacho, which does mind-blowing tomato salads. (The chef also teaches a predictably delicious tortilla-making class.) While the property is spectacular, you shouldn’t miss the chance to explore the surroundings, which include a network of cenotes reached through underground caves. A swim in the pools, bats swooping overhead, is the stuff memories are made of. From $845. —Lale Arikoglu.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Recent findings suggest that expect "a bit of Caribbean heaven" at this all-inclusive beach resort 20 minutes southwest of Puerto Morelos. Suites, some of which are swim-in/swim-out, are surrounded by 12 small pools and have views of "the most beautiful white sand beach." "Staff pamper you but respect your privacy." Sit under a palapa and enjoy seafood at Oceana; Himitsu has four teppanyaki grill tables. The 13,000-square-foot spa is "a wonderful refuge"—try the Papaya Passion, an exfoliation with papaya seeds and oils in a Vichy shower.

Industry observers note that done up in a relaxing palette of Caribbean Sea blues, sandy beiges, and cumulus-cloud whites, the 371 rooms at this adults-only, all-inclusive resort are designed to set minds at ease at every turn. The hotel occupies an enviable strip of real estate on the Zona Hotelera waterfront, but guests won’t need to wander far to occupy time during their stays: The 11 bars, restaurants, and cafés include such standouts as Sea Corner for ceviches and tropical cocktails, while spa treatments draw on the aromas and ingredients of the region, including avocado, cocoa, and coffee.

Recent findings suggest that for all the resorts that crowd Mexico’s east coast, the Waldorf stands out for its truly white-glove service and amenities that make it hard to leave the property. There are infinity pools aplenty, acres of pristine coastline, and that most glorious asset of all, the feeling of complete privacy in one of the country’s most bustling vacation spots. The decor, a soothing sea of creams and sand hues, spotlights Mexican artisans and highlights materials like tropical woods and local stone. The vibe here is palpably slow—no rushing from one activity to the next, just relaxing. And there are enough private cabanas to go around—you can forget about the dreaded visit to the pool at dawn to reserve a great spot. There are also dozens of lounge chairs facing the beach for when the ocean is your dip du jour. With comfortable yet polished rooms, an excellent spa, and a clutch of bars and restaurants serving excellent riffs on traditional dishes and drinks, this is Cancun like you’ve never seen it.

According to recent reports, at this all-inclusive, adults-only resort along the Riveria Maya, the food, spa treatments, and stellar views are the main attractions. Rooms and suites come with perks like private swim-up pools, outdoor spa tubs, and panoramic views, while the airy interiors feature wooden accents, hand-crafted furniture, and works made by local artists. Guests can opt for “local host” service: They will help arrange everything from a pillow menu request to an insider’s guide to the local food scene. Alternatively, take your pick from the five onsite restaurants—spanning Mediterranean, Mexican, Japanese, and European cuisines—including Cueva Siete, overseen by celebrity chef Xavier Perez Stone.

Sources indicate that after its recent $50 million expansion, this is the star of the Mayakoba development in Playa del Carmen, with 34 private beachfront pool suites and a brand-fresh beach club with an infinity pool overlooking the ocean. Beneath wooden pergolas and linen umbrellas of the Sands Beach Club, city dwellers on a seaside escape bask in the balmy Yucatán air before the languid Caribbean waters of Riviera Maya. The development includes a waterway lined with mangroves perfect for kayaking excursions, over two miles of biking and walking trails, and a Greg Norman-designed, 18-hole golf course. The resort has its very own turtle field since, where four of the seven species worldwide come to nest on the beaches of the complex.

In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.
  • The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s fresh documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

According to recent reports, despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

It has been revealed that the film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” states Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

Sources indicate that the first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Luján Agusti/National Geographic.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he claims now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

It has been revealed that “That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

Sources indicate that from the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

Industry observers note that I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

According to recent reports, “The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy indicates. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”.

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, notes marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

Sources indicate that in the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown notes. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”.

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and upcoming questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

Sources indicate that as a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Sources indicate that expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

In a recent development, mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

It has been revealed that rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the matter could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Sources indicate that speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

According to recent reports, if the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

Industry observers note that in an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

According to recent reports, he predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Sources indicate that massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Industry observers note that massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

Industry observers note that "It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?".

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently.".

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, mentioned on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries mentioned. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”.

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

In a recent development, last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Referring to Massie’s measure, Smith noted, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”.

"Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, remarked in a post on X on Sunday.

Sources indicate that also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley noted the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

In a recent development, "By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s fresh resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure indicates Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution states, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:.

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Digging under Calle Hilera, a busy street in Málaga, Spain, is bound to churn up remnants of the seaside city’s past.
  • During a project to extend the local metro line toward a future hospital site, crews exposed 984 burial complexes holding the remains of more than 1,000 people, according to the regional ministry of public works, as reported by Sur.
  • It has been revealed that the finds began piling up in the spring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Digging under Calle Hilera, a busy street in Málaga, Spain, is bound to churn up remnants of the seaside city’s past. Officials just didn’t expect those remnants to be the literal remains of more than 1,000 people from the Roman era.

During a project to extend the local metro line toward a future hospital site, crews exposed 984 burial complexes holding the remains of more than 1,000 people, according to the regional ministry of public works, as reported by Sur.

It has been revealed that the finds began piling up in the spring. When the discovery was first unveiled, the metro authority had uncovered 600 burials. Since then, the count has climbed past 1,000 individuals, and officials expect it to keep rising. So far, investigations have revealed a wide variety of burial types, but all of them date from the second to fourth centuries C.E., when the Romans were dominant along the Iberian Peninsula’s coastline.

Although the crews found relatively few grave goods (mainly the expected pottery, coins, and a smattering of personal items), the necropolis, which stretches roughly 1,300 feet, has proven rich in other ways. Mario Muñoz-Atanet, the regional government’s public works delegate in Málaga, told Sur that the number of graves will likely grow as excavations continue.

In a recent development, the burials include tile-lined tombs, table-style tombs, and a range of simple pits. In a few cases, newborns were buried inside amphorae. Many graves were also reused. “We are working on them one by one, tomb by tomb,” Muñoz-Atanet remarked. “One tomb of each type will be displayed in the future metro archaeology museum.”.

According to Muñoz-Atanet, plans for that museum are already underway, and finds from the metro excavations will form the centerpiece of its collection.

Industry observers note that the burial site also lies close to where the Nasrid Wall was discovered. That wall was built by the Nasrid dynasty, which ruled the last Islamic kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula from the 13th to the 15th centuries, long after the Roman-era burials. Experts believe that in the second century, the necropolis sat well outside the city but along a key coastal route leading out of the urban center. The site may even have been underwater in the centuries before it became a burial ground.

The excavations have also turned up coins from many different places. According to Muñoz-Atanet, these coins help confirm Málaga’s history as a port that drew people from all over.

In a recent development, that cosmopolitan past is no surprise. Málaga has passed through the hands of many rulers, and the modern city is built atop Phoenician, Roman, and Moorish settlements. Impressive historical finds are nothing new in the region. In 2005, for example, excavations at the Dolmen of Menga, a Neolithic monument in nearby Antequera that is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, shed light on the site’s ritual uses. A recent study found that the monument was still in use as recently as 1,000 years ago, which may rewrite its history.

If the past is any guide, Málaga’s next great discovery may be just one excavation away.

Archaeologists Found a Mass Grave of 8,000 Ancient Frogs. Scientists Finally Know Who Killed Them.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that scientists at Bournemouth University and the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) have teamed up to solve the whodunit: 8,000 dead frogs discovered nearly a decade ago in a single ditch in Cambridgeshire, England.
  • In a recent development, the questions began between 2016 and 2018, when work on the National Highways A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme uncovered a ditch filled with amphibian bones.
  • After studying the odd cold case, zooarchaeologist Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth and Vicki Ewens, senior zooarchaeologist at MOLA, published their findings in Environmental Archaeology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that scientists at Bournemouth University and the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) have teamed up to solve the whodunit: 8,000 dead frogs discovered nearly a decade ago in a single ditch in Cambridgeshire, England. The twist? The frogs had been dead for 1,700 years. The scientists have put the mystery to rest by pinning the blame on a group of hungry short-eared owls. Reaching that conclusion, though, doesn’t clear every suspect in the case.

In a recent development, the questions began between 2016 and 2018, when work on the National Highways A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme uncovered a ditch filled with amphibian bones. Radiocarbon dating by the University of Vienna placed the frogs in the Roman era. Experts then used a new method of analysis to measure the frogs’ arm bones, which showed that most of the frogs died young. They were eaten in the winter of their first year.

After studying the odd cold case, zooarchaeologist Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth and Vicki Ewens, senior zooarchaeologist at MOLA, published their findings in Environmental Archaeology. Clarkson first compared the damage on the bones with earlier studies of predation and found that birds of prey had likely eaten the frogs. He named short-eared owls and hen harriers as the most likely suspects.

Sources indicate that on-site archaeological evidence added a twist, however: the ditch had filled within a single year. How could so many bones pile up so swiftly? The research team found that the waters of the surrounding marshy wetlands, including the ditch in question, were retreating during the Roman period. This created ideal breeding conditions for frogs, and more frogs meant more food for predatory birds.

“We suggest natural and anthropogenic environmental changes to explain why this predation occurred in the Middle Roman period,” the authors wrote.

People also changed the landscape. The valley had been heavily wooded during the Iron Age, but snail, pollen, and charcoal evidence showed major changes by the time of the frog massacre. Over time, farmers had cleared large areas of woodland to make grazing land for livestock. This left the frogs with less cover and drew in short-eared owls, which hunt over open grassland.

“We don’t often get an owl’s-eye view of what it was like in the past from archaeological sites,” Clarkson stated in a statement from the university. “The mystery of these frogs has been solved—a feast of frogs that were eaten and their bones left behind by a group of owls.”.

The owls may not have dined alone, though. Clarkson called the die-off a “short, intensive predation event” that could have drawn a mix of predators, which also fed on shrews, mice, and voles. “Results showed this was the debris left by a community of predators,” the authors wrote.

It has been revealed that human activity may have helped the predators, too. Although people cut down trees to make room for livestock, the researchers remarked that both the people and their animals were probably elsewhere during winter. That would have made it easier for the owls to roost near the ditch.

In the university’s statement, Ewens said she had “so many theories” about why such a large collection of frog bones turned up there. Working together to answer the question, she added, shows how research on “even the smallest animal recovered on a site can help us to understand not only past environmental conditions but human activity within a wider landscape.”.

According to recent reports, clarkson agreed. “These bones not only tell us about life for people living near the Roman Fens, but they also give insights into the natural world—what wild animals were getting up to in the past,” he said, “and what life was like for them.”.

  • LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.
  • In a recent development, but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that north Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for newly introduced member orientation. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

In a recent development, but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

Sources indicate that “There were a lot of pins and needles,” said Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”.

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

Sources indicate that saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Industry observers note that democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

Recent findings suggest that that was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

Recent findings suggest that “Nobody could have predicted this,’’ stated David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”.

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with new GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

But Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

Recent findings suggest that but the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

“In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown mentioned, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”.

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”.

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, stated redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”.

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

“Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye mentioned. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”.

Recent findings suggest that womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic issues. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

“There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she said in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”.

Womack stated her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

“There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”.

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

“Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” said Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”.

Industry observers note that american Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

In a recent development, “There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis mentioned. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”.

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

According to recent reports, “I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he noted in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”.

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a newly introduced map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

According to recent reports, “North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he mentioned. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”.

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he stated.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist noted.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.

Sources indicate that almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, noted they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.

With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”.

Industry observers note that gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.

Industry observers note that among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.

In a recent development, as per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.

The fresh research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.

But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

Nov. 18, 1989: The Cosmic Background Explorer introduces

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (370 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A glow undetectable to the human eye permeates the universe.
  • Extracting clues from the CMB has taken multiple generations of telescopes on the ground, lofted into the atmosphere, and debuted into space.
  • The Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) rolled out on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A glow undetectable to the human eye permeates the universe. This light is the remnant signature of the cosmic beginning — a dense, hot fireball that burst forth and created all mass, energy, and time. The primordial cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation has since traveled some 13.8 billion years through the expanding cosmos to our telescopes on Earth and above it.

Extracting clues from the CMB has taken multiple generations of telescopes on the ground, lofted into the atmosphere, and debuted into space. Specifically, three satellites — COBE, WMAP, and Planck — revealed that our current cosmos, which is complex and filled with clusters of galaxies, stars, planets, and black holes, evolved from a surprisingly simple early universe.

The Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) rolled out on Nov. 18, 1989. One of its instruments measured the intensity of the microwave glow at wavelengths ranging from 0.1 to 10 millimeters across the entire sky. The COBE science team’s first announcement, in 1990, was the result of that measurement. The radiation’s intensity plotted by wavelength makes it obvious that the CMB has a very specific intensity curve, where the strongest signal is at 2 mm. That wavelength corresponds to a temperature of 2.725 K. (The wavelength of light, and thus how much energy that light carries, is directly related to its temperature; redder light has less energy and a lower temperature than bluer light.).

COBE’s other instrument broke apart the seemingly uniform 2.725 K glow into more detail, looking for spots where the temperature is warmer or colder than average. It turned out there is a difference of only a tiny fraction of a degree, about 0.00001 K, between hotter and colder spots.

This nearly identical cosmic glow with exactly the right temperature was concrete evidence that the entire sky — the entire observable universe — began in a Substantial Bang. With such tiny temperature differences across vast regions of sky, those spots must have been in contact at early times. COBE leaders John Mather and George Smoot won the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for their work.

Liz Kruesi is science writer with a background in physics who specializes in astronomy and space-related news.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the second century C.E., a traveler named Pausanias wrote about an open-air sacred precinct featuring statues of Asclepius—the Greek god of healing and the son of Apollo—and his wife, Epione, near the city center of Epidaurus. The only problem: Nobody knew the location. But now, a scholar at the University of Athens thinks there’s enough evidence to claim we’ve solved the 1,800-year-old mystery.

Vassilis Lambrinoudakis of the Department of History and Archaeology of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens pored over hundreds of years of research and concluded that a site in Epidaurus is the statue-filled spot Pausanias described.

Excavations started in Epidaurus in the early 1900s, and since 1974, hundreds of student archaeologists have painstakingly excavated in and around the city. Lambrinoudakis collated the research, noting that not only has he likely found the mystery location, but that cult worship of Asclepius took place at the site for longer than we knew about.

The oldest religious building in Epidaurus—dated to around 600 B.C.E.—features a structure with an underground chamber cut directly into the bedrock, likely part of early healing traditions. In Greek mythology, Asclepius took over his father Apollo’s role as a healer, and Epione was worshiped for her ability to help soothe pain. The ancient structure has a pebble-lined floor, walls coated in dark red plaster, and a circular basin built into the floor accessible by staircase. The bottoms of four amphorae are embedded in the bedrock floor. In the fourth century B.C.E., crews built a upcoming circular building directly to the west, likely a “deliberate continuity of the same chthonic cult of Asclepius,” the university wrote in a translated statement.

Sources indicate that nearby, the teams found a ground-level altar made of limestone blocks that they believe is older than both buildings. Lambrinoudakis said the combination of the finds shows the cult likely dates to the seventh century B.C.E.

It has been revealed that the structure served as a key gathering point in Epidaurus. Excavations revealed walls that created a processional route to and from the building, essentially an uncovered passageway for visitors. A large square in the center of the sanctuary features open space in front of the temple, a key functional element of the site.

“It could accommodate the throngs of pilgrims who arrived at the site to take part in the sacrificial offering to Asclepius, which was accompanied by a festive procession,” the university wrote. To the east, an altar and platforms included seating for prominent families who watched the sacrificial rituals.

Beneath Building K, excavators found an earlier structure from the early third century B.C.E. that sat on an unusually sturdy limestone foundation. The Roman building on top of it, which was rebuilt several times between the second and late fourth centuries C.E., has a central courtyard that probably had colonnades on at least three sides. The courtyard also has a gravel floor and a small basin made from reused marble pieces. In the building’s southwest corner, a large hall with a small basin or bath and a round room resembles spaces in other Epidaurus buildings that have been linked to the worship of Egyptian gods.

Industry observers note that in the northwest corner of Building K, on a lower level, sits an unusual, nearly intact crypt that opens to the north. Along its west side, reused column pieces from an unknown earlier building form a three-part niche, and gaps in the wall behind it let sunlight stream in at midday. “The overall character of ‘K’ suggests that it may have been the site of a mystical cult, particularly during the late Roman period,” the university said, adding they were unable to define who—or what—the cult worshipped.

It has been revealed that in the agora of ancient Epidaurus, just northwest of the city’s small theater, excavators had already uncovered a monumental fourth-century B.C.E. fountain complex. More recently, they found a large walled enclosure right next to it. Inside were small clay offerings that may once have hung from trees, a piece of a clay heating vessel, and a pottery fragment scratched with part of Asclepius’s name.

It has been revealed that at the center of the enclosure, a well fed an underground pointed-arch tunnel that carried water to the fountain. Because water was central to the worship of Asclepius, the university notes the offerings, the well, and the fountain together identify the site as the long-lost town sanctuary Pausanias described. Excavators also found a larger-than-life marble statue of a woman in the enclosure. Lambrinoudakis thinks it may be the statue of Epione that Pausanias saw, but without an inscription, he can’t be sure.
