  • Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

AI is already powering upcoming, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a fresh worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

The results hint at a upcoming way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”.

Here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

It has been revealed that historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, claims Guan, of the University of Toronto.

According to recent reports, that adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments indicated. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

According to recent reports, and there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.).

Recent findings suggest that most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan says. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI tech giant Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

“The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

Sources indicate that the Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” states cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Industry observers note that rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan says.

Sources indicate that guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

The octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a newly introduced device, the head would use AI to plan how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler notes. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

It has been revealed that an attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover latest places to copy itself (third image).

The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.).

The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan says they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers showed another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan states the company’s work indicates that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

In a recent development, and that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

It has been revealed that anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that demonstrated it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

It has been revealed that whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan states. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still big programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma says. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

It has been revealed that ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler says.

Industry observers note that guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”.

An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) keeps your essential devices temporarily online, which provides a window for you to hit send on that last-minute email.

While a standard power strip or surge protector offers sufficient, albeit basic, protection, a UPS ensures devices are properly shut down and are protected from data loss. Beyond just keeping your devices running, the best UPS battery backups also shield sensitive electronics from potentially damaging power surges and fluctuations throughout the day. Our personal experience and circumstances informed our choices, as we considered the models that could protect devices and provide sufficient battery backup during outages.

As we mentioned, it lacks more advanced features, including AVR, but it’s still a solid, affordable option.

This prevents potential corruption or data loss. The device also supports a graceful shutdown feature, which automatically shuts down connected equipment if you’re unable to do it when the connected devices reach a predetermined power level.

Industry observers note that the UPS offers both data line and coaxial line safeguards to give you extra peace of mind during power disturbances. An informative LCD screen on the front panel displays crucial information, such as battery capacity, load capacity, the number of power events that have occurred, and any system errors.

For added convenience, the UPS is equipped with both a USB-A and a USB-C port on the front to charge your phone or tablet in the same place as your home office equipment.

Industry observers note that most UPS devices take up a lot of floor or desk space. This one, however, measures approximately 4.1 by 10.8 by 5.5 inches, which is more compact than most for easier integration into your current home office.

It has been revealed that the UPS automatically switches off from the battery backup when your power comes back on. And when the time comes, you can replace its battery instead of replacing the entire unit.

There are some trade-offs to the more compact design. For instance, more advanced models contain a few more outlets. You also miss out on an LCD screen and AVR. However, these compromises bring the cost down on this space-efficient UPS.

Recent findings suggest that this CyberPower UPS easily integrates into a server setup because of its rack-mounting feature. The design makes it an excellent choice for small businesses that have a data center or server room, keeping the UPS close to the devices it’s protecting. It fits into racks as small as 14 inches in depth.

Industry observers note that the device features eight battery-backed outlets and an LCD panel, which displays information on battery and power conditions. The screen also shows alerts about potential issues before they affect your devices.

Like other CyberPower models, this one supports management software for monitoring the UPS remotely. Other features include data line protection and an estimated battery runtime of 10 minutes at half load.

In a recent development, most UPS models offer limited battery life, even at half load, which isn’t ideal for IT professionals or network administrators. This APC model, however, delivers impressive battery runtime, with up to 23 minutes at half load in the event of an outage. That’s almost double what other top models offer, giving you ample time to save your work and safely shut down your devices.

In a recent development, A traditional UPS buys you a few minutes, just enough time to save your work and shut down. If the power's out for hours, you need something bigger. The Anker Solix S2000 is a portable power station that doubles as a UPS: Plug it into the wall, plug your gear into it, and when the power cuts out, it switches to battery power in under 10 milliseconds, fast enough for most home office setups.

And it can keep going for a long time. In our testing, the S2000 ran a refrigerator for just over 24 hours on its 2,010 watt-hours of capacity, and a typical home office draws far less. The UPS you choose should come with enough outlets to accommodate all the devices you need to plug in, with some room for additional devices in the future. Pay attention to the distinction between battery-backed outlets, which offer surge protection and battery power during outages, and surge-protected-only outlets, which, as the name suggests, only offer surge protection.

According to recent reports, every model we write about offers surge protection as a standard feature, even on outlets that don’t offer battery power. Batteries enable a UPS to power your devices once the grid fails. That’s why it’s essential to choose a UPS with enough battery-backed outlets to support the devices you want to keep online.

More advanced UPS models typically offer more outlets (and more that are battery-backed). For example, the more affordable Amazon Basics Standby UPS 600VA has eight outlets, four of which have battery backup, while the more advanced CyberPower CP1500AVRLCD3 has 12 outlets, six of which have battery backup. In addition to AC outlets, some UPS models have USB-A or USB-C ports to connect your smartphone and other devices. These ports easily charge your devices without taking up an outlet.

It’s also notable to ensure replacing the battery on the UPS you choose is straightforward and easy. This simplifies maintenance and increases the device’s lifespan. Advanced UPS models typically include battery health monitoring features, so you’ll get a heads up when a battery nears the end of its life.

Recent findings suggest that on average, UPS batteries last three to five years before needing replacement, though this lifespan varies depending on usage. Automatic Voltage Regulation, or AVR, stabilizes inconsistent incoming voltage. It converts fluctuating voltage from the power source into a steady, consistent output for connected devices. This protects sensitive electronics from power irregularities without relying on the UPS battery.

It has been revealed that as a bonus, AVR reduces wear and tear on the battery, potentially extending its lifespan. Not all models include this feature, particularly those priced on the lower end.

During an outage, a UPS inverter converts the direct current (DC) stored in its battery into the alternating current (AC) that devices expect. Pure sine wave models output a smooth wave that closely matches utility power. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD lists sine wave output on battery and is designed for active PFC power supplies. The APC BR1500MS2 lists sine wave output on battery with a transfer time of as little as eight seconds.

Sources indicate that during an outage, a UPS inverter converts the direct current (DC) stored in its battery into the alternating current (AC) that devices expect. Power from the wall doesn’t just switch on and off. Its voltage rises and falls in a smooth, rounded curve called a sine wave, swinging from positive to negative and back 60 times a second.

Pure sine wave models output a smooth wave that closely matches utility power, so your devices run on battery the same way they run on the grid. Some models output a simulated sine wave instead, a stepped signal that switches between positive and negative voltage with brief rests at zero. That output works for basic electronics, but it could cause problems for more sensitive electronics, like audio equipment and desktop PCs.

According to recent reports, desktop PCs are the biggest concern. Most use power supplies with active power factor correction (PFC), a circuit that improves efficiency and helps the unit meet energy standards. On a simulated sine wave, some of these power supplies can shut down unexpectedly or run under extra strain. Most devices without active PFC, including modems and routers, can handle a simulated wave without trouble during a typical short outage.

For a gaming PC, workstation, or home theater system, a pure sine wave UPS is the safer bet. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD lists sine wave output on battery and is designed for active PFC power supplies. The APC BR1500MS2 lists sine wave output on battery with a transfer time of as little as 8 milliseconds.

Industry observers note that having a display on a UPS may seem like a luxury, but it’s very helpful to have some kind of indicator to give you insight into battery status. Compact and budget models, like the APC BE600M1, typically stick to a few status lights that tell you whether the unit is running on wall power or battery.

An LCD screen shows measurements such as battery charge, how much power your devices are drawing, input and output voltage, and, most importantly, estimated runtime. That last one comes in clutch during an outage, since it tells you exactly how many minutes you have to save your work and shut down.

The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD's color screen tilts upward, so it's easier to read when the UPS sits on the floor under your desk, and the APC BR1500MS2 keeps a running count of the power events it has handled. And if your UPS lives in a bedroom, check whether you can dim or turn off the backlight. A glowing screen is useful during an outage, but less so at 2 a.m. when you’re trying to sleep.

Industry observers note that A cable that’s at least five feet long offers greater flexibility in terms of where you place your UPS. A five-foot-long cable reaches wall outlets that are farther away and positions the UPS conveniently for your devices. You’ll have the freedom to place the UPS in the best spot for your setup, such as under a desk or in a server rack. Remember, a short cable potentially limits where you place the UPS, so it’s always a good idea to go longer, not shorter.

UPS models that support management software give you greater control over the UPS from a phone or computer to remotely shut down connected devices, and some support “graceful shutdown,” which automatically shuts down connected equipment if you’re unable to do it when the connected devices reach a predetermined power level.

Other features worth considering include an LCD display to monitor a UPS’s status, expandable battery capacity, and an audible alarm during power disturbances.

Setting up a UPS is straightforward: Simply plug the UPS into a wall outlet and connect your devices to the UPS. This plug-and-play simplicity means a UPS device is great for anyone, no matter their level of technical know-how. But be aware of the following safety guidelines before powering on a UPS in your home office.

It has been revealed that companies advise against connecting devices like copiers, laser printers, or space heaters to a UPS, as these can overload the device. Instead, use a separate surge protector.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, never plug a UPS into a surge protector or vice versa. It’s also crucial to avoid plugging a UPS into an extension cord because this can potentially overload the cord and create a fire hazard. It’s recommended to always plug your UPS directly into a grounded wall outlet. Doing so will ensure your UPS operates safely while providing the best possible protection for your devices.

Finding the right UPS battery backup largely comes down to the total wattage you need to keep your computer up and running while you save and shut down. Speaking broadly, we'd tell you that most home office setups with a desktop PC, monitor, modem, and router should look for a UPS around 600 to 1500 volt-amperes (VA).

It has been revealed that to get a more accurate idea of what you specifically need, add up the wattage of all your connected devices, then look for a backup that can handle 120 to 130 percent of that load. That will give you enough time to shut down safely with some wiggle room in case you need to finish a task (or have something urgent come up before you can finish up).

Recent findings suggest that every system is different, but we'd expect a UPS in the 1000 to 1500VA range to keep your desktop and monitor running for about 15 minutes, which should be long enough to save and safely shut down. A smaller model can probably keep laptop-based setup for a similar amount of time, or power a modem and router for 30 to 45 minutes.

In a recent development, these are all broad estimates, though, and will vary based on what specific gear you're using. We recommend calculating your own power needs to figure out exactly how much time you'll have to shut down in the event of an emergency.

According to recent reports, yes, a UPS backup easily powers a router and modem, and this is one of the most common uses for a small unit. This type of hardware usually consumes only about 10 to 30 watts combined, which is relatively low when compared to computers or TVs. Because of this low draw, even a compact unit would be able to keep your internet running for 30 minutes or more during a power outage.

In a recent development, the phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll revision this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

In a recent development, A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope. The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

Recent findings suggest that the phases of the Moon are: Latest Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

RELATED: 20 things to see on the Moon.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Sources indicate that super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Sources indicate that blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four Latest Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

It has been revealed that harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

Industry observers note that what is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

Sources indicate that how does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

Many fields of science have struggled under the second Trump administration, with funding cuts and delays plaguing research in fields such as public health and climate science. But some topics have found firmer footing, including artificial intelligence and quantum science.

These technologies, along with supercomputing, “are going to be the three legs of the stool that is going to transform how science and engineering is done,” notes Darío Gil, undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy.

In November 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to launch the Genesis Mission, a $5 billion whole-of-government effort to advance science via artificial intelligence. The initiative began with the DOE but has since expanded to more than 15 federal agencies.

In June, the president issued an executive order that aims to accelerate the development of tools such as quantum computers, quantum sensors and quantum networks. And in July, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy issued a 123-page report describing its vision for a “golden age” of federal science, in which agencies align investments in research and development with administration priorities.

Federal agencies spent some $4.2 billion on AI R&D in 2025, according to an arm of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy that quantifies such investments.

According to recent reports, many scientists are enthusiastic about the opportunities for AI and quantum research. But some caution that a measured approach is needed. “My strongest opinion … is that I want to see all fields of science supported,” claims Brad Marston, a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. “Priorities have to be chosen, but getting a good balance is key, because you never know where some advance will come from.”.

Recent findings suggest that through Genesis, the DOE plans to use its troves of data as well as experimental and computing facilities to produce a common set of AI tools and a shared ecosystem for science. “That’s conceptually a very powerful idea,” notes astronomer Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. “And if it pans out as intended, it could drive great advances in science and technology.”.

It has been revealed that this year, DOE funded nearly 300 projects through Genesis — including one led by Mandelbaum. Her team’s effort aims to unify immense datasets from astronomical facilities around the world, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument and the Zwicky Transient Facility. That would enable AI models to be trained on the data, which could help uncover hidden astronomical insights.

Industry observers note that H. Stockebrand/RubinObs/NOIRLab/AURA/SLAC/DOE/NSF.

In a recent development, other projects include efforts to accelerate nuclear reactor development, create simulations of the U.S. electric grid and study nuclear fusion. And federal agencies including the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health have launched their own Genesis efforts, centered around the mission’s National Science and Technology Challenges, which include topics in health, biology, energy, space, national security and more.

Many scientists were already wielding AI in their work. But Genesis “really did create an inflection point,” claims John Sarrao, director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, Calif. SLAC is now involved with 20 Genesis projects and leads two.

It has been revealed that compared with AI, quantum technologies are less mature. With quantum computing, “we’re still at mile one or two or three of a marathon,” notes Celia Merzbacher, executive director of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium, a coalition of public and private institutions that works to bolster quantum tech in the United States. Nevertheless, researchers hope the two technologies can amplify one another. AI could help design and develop quantum computers, for example, while quantum computing shows promise for efficiently tackling certain machine learning problems.

Accordingly, several Genesis projects involve quantum error correction, quantum sensors and quantum materials. And the DOE’s Quantum Genesis initiative aims to develop scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computers by 2028.

Industry observers note that AI and quantum were not always hot topics. “Both of those areas … were kind of backwaters until recent advances,” Marston notes. Before the development of deep neural networks, for example, AI was mostly a curiosity. “It points to the importance of having a balanced approach to science funding,” he says. What starts as an obscure scientific specialty may suddenly explode into wide relevance.

Sources indicate that in the context of limited resources, prioritizing one area of research necessitates deprioritizing another. While some funding for the DOE’s portion of Genesis came from the One Big Beautiful Bill passed in 2025, much of the rest came from the DOE’s budget.

As excited as Mandelbaum is about Genesis, she is concerned about funding for non-AI related work. A cosmology grant her group received from the DOE didn’t align with Genesis mission priorities and was reduced this year, she notes. “If the reality is that some of this [funding] is coming out of the baseline research budget in my field, then I think that it would be beneficial for the DOE to engage the scientific community about those trade-offs,” Mandelbaum says.

In response to these concerns, Gil claims that the money going to Genesis from the DOE’s Office of Science — about $400 million so far — is small compared to the office’s total FY2026 budget of $8.4 billion.

Recent findings suggest that sarrao claims that it’s vital to build on the momentum of Genesis while still supporting the DOE’s core research. His impression is that things are trending in the right direction. “Are there really exciting opportunities? Yes, 100 percent,” Sarrao says. “Are there risks if you get the balance wrong? Equally well, 100 percent.”.

Nov. 19, 1969: Apollo 12 lands on the Moon

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (258 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 14, 1969, launch amid stormy skies, Apollo 12’s Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed on the Moon in Oceanus Procellarum (the Ocean of Storms).
  • Sources indicate that although Bean accidentally pointed their color TV camera at the Sun, damaging it, both the Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) were otherwise successful.
  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Five days after their Nov. 14, 1969, launch amid stormy skies, Apollo 12’s Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed on the Moon in Oceanus Procellarum (the Ocean of Storms). Part of Apollo 12’s mission was to demonstrate improvements to the precision of lunar landings, and Conrad piloted the Intrepid Lunar Module to a pinpoint landing on Nov. 19. While their crewmate Richard Gordon remained in the Command Module (Yankee Clipper) above them, Conrad and Bean began the first of their two moonwalks. Conrad descended the ladder from the LM first, and as he stepped onto the Moon quipped, “Whoopie! Man, that may have been a small one for Neil, but that’s a long one for me.”.

Sources indicate that although Bean accidentally pointed their color TV camera at the Sun, damaging it, both the Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) were otherwise successful. The astronauts collected rock and soil samples and deployed their Apollo Lunar Surface Experiment Package (ALSEP), which included a solar wind collector, and seismometer, and a magnetometer. They also visited the Surveyor 3 unmanned lander (which had been on the Moon since 1967), retrieving several components of the spacecraft to return to Earth for study. After 31 and a half hours on the Moon, nearly eight hours of those spent in EVAs, Intrepid lifted off and re-docked with Yankee Clipper. The crew safely splashed down back on Earth on Nov. 24.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

“A quest is a search and an adventure,” reads the opening salvo of the September 1976 Popular Mechanics cover story, “7 Great Quests of Man.” Admittedly, this is a somewhat muted, almost “Maid of Honor Reads the Webster’s Dictionary Definition of Love for Her Toast”-esque opener to place beneath such a grandiose headline.

In defense of that half-century-old article, finding a really great opening line for a story can be hard. That’s as true now as it was 50 years ago. At least the author didn’t take the easy way out and just start it by quoting somebody else instead.

But what of the “Great Quests” themselves? Have any of them been conquered in the last half-century? Have any of the tools and technologies developed since 1976 brought us a smidge closer to solving these age-old mysteries?

To mark the 50th anniversary of the “7 Great Quests of Man,” we took a look back at the quests that captivated readers in 1976, and how close we’ve come to bringing them to an end since then.

According to recent reports, the first Great Quest on the list is one of the oldest, the search for the lost continent of Atlantis. The earliest extant record of the story of Atlantis was penned by Plato, who put the words in the mouth of his interlocutor Critias in a pair of dialogues written around 360 B.C.E.

By 1976, Atlantis was having a moment in the sun (one whose rays could presumably reach its watery depths). Paranormal phenomena researcher Charles Berlitz’s book The Mystery of Atlantis was back on bookshelves in a new paperback edition, and on television, everyone from Leonard Nimoy to Jabberjaw was seemingly in search of the sunken continent.

In “7 Great Quests of Man,” after dismissing the claims of a psychic who said Atlantis would rise again, we actually offered up a different theory: that Atlantis had already been found back in the 1960s, and it was actually a volcanic island called Santorini.

It has been revealed that at the time, we dated the eruption to sometime between 1480 and 1450 B.C.E. Modern radiocarbon evidence suggests it happened more than a century earlier, likely around 1600 B.C.E. Either way, the blast caused a large part of the island to sink, leaving only three smaller islands above water (including the largest, now called Thera or Santorini).

“During the 1960s excavations of Thera revealed that it had once been the home of the Minoans,” we wrote, “These were a highly civilized, seafaring people whose center was on the island of Crete about 70 miles from Santorini. The Minoans on Thera had been wiped out by the eruption. The well-preserved ruins now being uncovered are one of the major archaeological finds of this century.”.

Industry observers note that here in the 21st century, Santorini is actually still making waves, literally. We reported last year that magma from the island’s crust caused a remarkable 25,000 tremors in just a 30-day period. And while advancements in tech like sonar have yet to turn up any evidence of Atlantis, intrepid adventurers have uncovered several other sunken cities, from the relics of Canopus and the Sanctuary of Poseidon at Samikon to the medieval city of Shipden and the “Atlantis of the Sands,” Ubar.

Next up on the list was Noah’s Ark. That readers in 1976 were dying to know where Noah’s Ark was is actually no surprise; it would be the same as folks in 2026 wanting to find the Trojan Horse after seeing The Odyssey. That’s because in 1976, a documentary called In Search of Noah’s Ark proved a box-office sensation, becoming one of the top ten highest-grossing films of the year.

In a recent development, part of the film’s appeal was the sentiment that the remnants of the Biblical vessel could well be hidden away on Turkey’s Mount Ararat, and only the political strife of our modern times was keeping us from finding the ancient treasure. After all, during this time, the United States had actually implemented an arms embargo on Turkey after its actions in Cyprus in 1974, so things were undoubtedly fraught geopolitically in the region.

It has been revealed that “7 Great Quests of Man” suggests as much. “Currently the Turkish government is discouraging foreign expeditions to Mount Ararat,” it concludes, “it’s in a politically sensitive area.” Back then, we said that Ark hunters would no doubt return to the site “as soon as restrictions are lifted,” which is the kind of thing you casually say when you don’t realize there’s about to be a violent military coup in four years.

In a recent development, now, in the 21st century, some progress has actually been made in the search for Noah’s Ark. In October 2026, we reported that soil samples were taken from Mount Ararat’s Durupinar formation, a peculiar geological feature in the area that’s long been considered a potential resting place for the Biblical vessel. The preliminary tests showed a high concentration of organic material, such as wood. Further lab work is being undertaken to try and determine “if man-made activity or decaying wood sit in the soil.”.

In a recent development, “The hottest quest going in 1976 is the quest for the Loch Ness monster,” we wrote in “7 Great Quests of Man,” and that was no joke. 1976 really was Nessie’s year, with coverage of the alleged cryptid even appearing in the pages of the MIT Technology Review and the Fresh York Times.

Why was the Loch Ness Monster having such a moment during the Bicentennial? Simple: In 1975, new photographs purportedly showing the creature had surfaced. While we’re all familiar with the famous 1930s photo of Nessie’s alleged neck rising above the water, the two new pictures came courtesy of an underwater camera, and seemed to show the creature close up and beneath the waves. “One shows a close-up of what may be the head of an unknown animal,” we wrote in 1976, “the other what may be its head, neck and body.”.

Back then, we cited numerous notable biologists who felt the images were “sufficiently suggestive of a large aquatic animal” and concluded that “the long search may be nearing a conclusion.”.

Industry observers note that back in 2013, Scientific American blamed the photos’ appeal on pareidolia, our brain’s habit of finding faces and figures where there are none. The photo that was thought to show Nessie’s head “is most likely a gnarly tree-stump on the loch floor.”.

That being noted, the last few years have still yielded some interesting Loch Ness Monster talk, from a 2025 study concluding that Nessie wouldn’t look like you think (if it exists at all) to the recent recovery of a 1970s Loch Ness Monster trap with its own underwater camera (which captured no Nessie pictures, unfortunately).

So, in a sense, the Loch Ness Monster mystery is kind of like the Starland Vocal Band’s “Afternoon Delight.” It’s still around on the periphery today, and we’re all a little confused as to why it was such a major thing back in ’76.

For decades, man pondered two questions:.

2) Could Bigfoot beat the Six Million Dollar Man in a fight?

And in 1976, one of those questions was finally answered. In a two-part episode of The Six Million Dollar Man called “The Secret of Bigfoot,” Steve Austin (the character played by Lee Majors, not the professional wrestler) faced off against Bigfoot (played by André the Giant, the actual professional wrestler). Believe it or not, this was just one small component of the Bigfoot craze that overtook America in the 1970s. There were Bigfoot movies, Bigfoot TV shows, a Bigfoot board game and, unbeknownst to the average American, the FBI was even actively investigating the legitimacy of hairs that reportedly came from Sasquatch himself.

For real, Bigfoot has an FBI file, and we read it.

As our article pointed out back then, while talk of Yetis and Sasquatches originated near the start of the 20th century, 1970s Bigfoot mania was ignited by the famed Patterson-Gimlin film. You know the one. You’ve undoubtedly seen it. Back in 1967, amateur monster hunters Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin went out into the woods with a camera and captured footage of a seven-foot-tall creature covered in hair strolling by. While some were skeptical of the footage, thinking it was just a guy in a suit, back in 1976 our writer spoke to a primate expert at the Smithsonian Institution who mentioned, “I could not see the zipper and I still can’t.”.

Now in 2026, though, you can see the zipper if you want—in a manner of speaking, anyway.

Sources indicate that we don’t want to bum out the Bigfoot believers here. Look, maybe there is still a Sasquatch out there somewhere—and if you ask that one guy, there certainly was one, but it’s dead now). But as for the Patterson-Gimlin film? That received a thorough debunking in 2026 thanks to the revelatory documentary Capturing Bigfoot. The film, which debuted at SXSW in March 2026, confirms that the famous footage was a hoax, revealing never-before-seen “rehearsal footage” shot by the men in 1966, featuring a different design for the Sasquatch.

Recent findings suggest that “Oak Island, a small island on Mahone Bay off the coast of Nova Scotia, is the site of what has to be the most frustrating quest of modern times,” we wrote back in 1976. “There may be a treasure on the island. People have known where the treasure is buried for nearly 200 years. But it is so cleverly protected that all attempts to recover it have been foiled.”.

From the supposed “Money Pit” to the cipher stone to the Oak Island Curse, this north-of-the-border treasure hunt has built up its own glossary of lore and lingo over the last two centuries as eager treasure hunters braved booby traps in search of a historic payday. Popular Mechanics first covered the Oak Island treasure hunt 100 years ago, in the March 1926 story “Hunting Hidden Treasures,” and its allure attracted the attention of major names like John Wayne and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Here in 2026, we can say that the Oak Island mystery stands out from the other “Great Quests” outlined in our pages 50 years ago for one specific reason: the “7 Great Quests of Man” list itself had a direct influence on the current-day search for answers about Oak Island.

Industry observers note that how do we know that? Well, the new faces of the Oak Island treasure hunt mentioned so themselves.

“Growing up, I loved that magazine. Absolutely loved that magazine,” Marty Lagina told us. “There is one connection to Popular Mechanics too, aside from our interest in the magazine,” brother Rick Lagina chimed in. “There was an article in Popular Mechanics about Oak Island.” The two men are the stars of the long-running television series The Curse of Oak Island, currently airing its 14th season. While they’ve yet to uncover some massive trove at the bottom of the much-discussed Money Pit, the show’s efforts have helped uncover some of the island’s previously undocumented history, and the series’ popularity has kept the mysterious island in the cultural zeitgeist.

“Did visitors from other planets come to earth in ancient times?” we asked in 1976. Then we answered: “Recently, yes has become a very popular answer to that question.” And this was no exaggeration. People really were all in on this theory in the 1970s, and not just the fringe conspiracy crowd.

To give you an idea of just how pervasive alien fever was, we need to touch on a film called Chariots of the Gods. Based on the pseudoscientific work of Erich von Däniken, this 1970 documentary laid out the theory that the world’s religions and early human development were all influenced by ancient extraterrestrial visitors.

Recent findings suggest that how did audiences in the Disco Decade receive this claim? Well, not only was the film a commercial success, it actually managed to get an Academy Award nomination for Best Documentary Feature that year, putting it up alongside the historic concert film Woodstock and the MLK documentary King: A Filmed Record... Montgomery to Memphis. That would be like if this year You Can See Everything had to compete against an episode of Ancient Aliens at the Oscars.

Supporters of the theory pointed to ancient constructions they felt couldn’t have been built with “primitive tools,” and massive monuments constructed that could only be seen properly from the skies. Skeptics claimed these “view-from-above” tributes were intended for gods in the heavens, but true believers said it was a message to aliens.

In our world today, the ancient alien theory still gets bandied about from time to time. Recently, we’ve covered phenomena like the “Black Knight” satellite and the Silurian hypothesis, both of which have attracted their fair share of fringe “it was aliens” theories. But arguably the greatest cultural cachet the conspiracy theory has today is the face we’re all picturing when we read the sentence “it was aliens.”.

You know who we’re talking about. You’ve seen the memes.

According to recent reports, author Giorgio Tsoukalos got the meme treatment all the way back in 2010 for his credulous role on the immensely popular television show Ancient Aliens. That series, which still airs today, took the torch of Chariots of the Gods and ran with it, keeping the “ancient aliens” theory in the popular discourse through 22 television seasons, a video game, and even an adjacent series in which audiences watch very stoned people watch the show. As a Great Quest, we’ve come no closer to finding proof of ancient aliens, but as a pop culture concept? The brand has literally never been stronger.

“Ask most scientists what they think of the ancient-astronaut theories, and they will just snort at you,” we wrote in 1976. “But that doesn’t mean that they don’t take the subject of intelligent life in space seriously. They do. They are now trying to contact extraterrestrial civilizations. That is the last, and perhaps the most exciting, quest of all.”.

It has been revealed that it’s likely the oldest of the “7 Great Quests of Man,” as well. For as long as mankind has been aware that there was more beyond our world, we’ve wondered if there’s anybody out there. Unlike the other quests, your Bigfoots and Noah’s Arks—which call for some credulity, some willingness to believe the thing is possible—to many people, the idea that there must be some other intelligent life out in our vast universe feels so plausible that it’s hard not to resist. Yet, despite how improbable it seems that mankind is really alone in the universe, no credible evidence has ever materialized that there’s intelligent life out there.

Sources indicate that A few years before our article was published, in 1972, Pioneer 10 took off from Cape Kennedy carrying a gold-covered plate with images of a man and a woman accompanied by diagrams that scientists hoped could be understood by any intelligent life it reached. It wasn’t the first attempt to contact alien life (Dr. Frank Drake debuted Project Ozma back in 1960), but the legendary Carl Sagan thought this “message in a bottle” approach might be the key to communicating with intelligent life among the stars.

In a recent development, in the 21st century, the search for intelligent life continues unabated, be it attempts to identify aliens moving about in our universe today, or searching for remnants of those who may have died off far in the distant past. At Pop Mech, we’ve continued to keep our eyes to the skies, while trying to contend with the perplexing Fermi Paradox—the question of why, in a universe billions of years old, we appear to be the only intelligent life to ever exist in it.

Yet, with all our new technology developed in the last 50 years, we still find ourselves gazing up at the stars and wondering who might be out there, just as we did when “7 Great Quests of Man” was written.

In a recent development, back then, we posited that our message would be heard by whatever life is out there. “It may happen a thousand years from now, or tomorrow.” We’ll check back in on that in another 50 years.

Hear stars being born in Chandra’s fresh sonifications

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that every image of the cosmos is a translation of data.
  • Sonification does the same for the ears, turning an object’s brightness, color, and position into pitch, volume, and tone.
  • Our ears are acutely sensitive to shifts in pitch, and researchers in fields ranging from astronomy to volcanology have found that listening to data can reveal patterns a visual plot might hide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that every image of the cosmos is a translation of data. The X-rays collected by NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the infrared light gathered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) are invisible to our eyes, so astronomers assign them colors we can see. Even optical observations, from Hubble to backyard astrophotographers, translate, too, often assigning or enhancing color based on emission in various filters.

Sonification does the same for the ears, turning an object’s brightness, color, and position into pitch, volume, and tone. The idea dates back at least to the Geiger counter, invented in 1908, whose clicks intensify as radiation climbs. In 2020, the Chandra X-ray Center launched A Universe of Sound, NASA’s first ongoing program to sonify astronomical data.

Our ears are acutely sensitive to shifts in pitch, and researchers in fields ranging from astronomy to volcanology have found that listening to data can reveal patterns a visual plot might hide. Sonification also opens the cosmos to people who are blind or have low vision, for whom a processed image offers little.

RELATED: Listen to the universe: How sonification turns data into sound.

On November 17, Chandra released four latest sonifications, each built on a region where stars are forming right now. Young, massive stars blast out X-rays in fierce winds and outbursts, and studying those nurseries helps astronomers reconstruct how stars — the Sun included — got their start. Each piece pairs Chandra’s X-ray data with views from other NASA telescopes.

Recent findings suggest that each sonification plays as a short video. A line sweeps across the image, and whatever it crosses becomes sound. Most of the regions also come in three versions — Chandra’s X-rays alone, the companion telescope’s data alone, and the full composite. Try a single layer first, then the composite, and you’ll start to hear which sounds are associated with which kind of light.

At around 400 light-years away, the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex is the closest star-forming region of the four. This crowded region is filled with a wide variety of stars. Chandra’s X-ray data identifies individual newborn stars, while JWST maps the other stars, gas, and dust around them. The X-rays ring out as bright, shimmering notes. Meanwhile, the clouds of dust and gas provide shifting ethereal chords, and individual stars land as crisp, percussive pings. Listen for the hush partway through — that’s a stretch of dark dust that hides almost all light.

About 1,310 light-years away and just below Orion’s Belt, the Orion Nebula is often visible to the naked eye and shows up in even the smallest telescope on a dark night. Chandra reveals more than 1,000 young stars here, each one sparkling in the sonification. Around them, the nebula’s diffuse X-ray glow holds steady as a ringing whistle. JWST’s infrared view of the dust and gas is audible as bent, warbling strings and a synthesized harp, reaching a crescendo in the nebula’s densest region before fading out.

Roughly 7,670 light-years away lies the ridge of gas and dust that became one of JWST’s most famous images when it was released in 2022. Chandra sees the scene differently, cutting through the dust to the hidden infant stars within it. Each of those stars plays as a quick stab, while the region’s faint X-ray glow draws out droning, unhurried notes — all played on an actual cello by musician Johnny Mok. JWST’s towering cliffs are a steady drone underneath, with new instruments chiming in briefly to denote a star or one of the cliffline’s jagged peaks.

Some 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major, M82 is the only object in the album beyond our galaxy. This starburst galaxy is building stars many times faster than the Milky Way. Its newborn giants burn out and explode promptly, venting superheated gas plumes that shine brightly in Chandra’s X-rays. Here, Chandra’s data joins Hubble’s visible-light view and infrared from JWST and the retired Spitzer Space Telescope. X-rays sit at the very top of the register, with the region’s busy center whooshing like moving air, filling most of the audible spectrum. It is punctuated by sharp, short stings from brighter newborn stars. The infrared rumbles below as a low hum interrupted by picked notes, and visible light fills the middle with a variety of sounds, including sweeping chords that rise and fall with optical brightness.

In a recent development, the Chandra sonifications come from a team led by visualization scientist Kimberly Arcand of the Chandra X-ray Center, working with astrophysicist Matt Russo and musician Andrew Santaguida of the SYSTEM Sounds project and consultant Christine Malec, a blind astronomer and musician. You can hear all four at the Chandra release page, and find the program’s full back catalog at chandra.si.edu/sound.

Where Chandra’s fresh album is composed by others, Skysynth lets you become the composer. Built by the same SYSTEM Sounds duo of Russo and Santaguida for the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s SkyViewer app, it lets you roam Rubin’s ultra-wide view of the southern sky — press Play to coast, or steer with your arrow keys or by dragging with the mouse. Galaxies crossing the center of the screen strum a harp and stars ring a glockenspiel, with color setting the pitch and brightness the volume.

Try it at skyviewer.app/skysynth.

According to recent reports, brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#7139. Industry News: What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

Industry News: What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a fresh set of patients.
  • Kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a fresh set of patients. They show up at the University of Kansas Health System hospital in Kansas City with what looks like severe opiate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting and muscle aches. They’re extremely anxious and sometimes hallucinating. But they haven’t taken an opioid, like fentanyl or heroin. Instead, they’ve used something labeled as kratom, though it may not contain kratom at all.

Kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids. But souped-up fresh versions with hyperpotent derivatives of the active compound are sold online and in gas stations. The derivatives act strongly on the body’s opioid receptors and are often far more powerful than the opioid drugs they are sometimes intended to replace. Kratom products — sold as pills, liquid shots, edibles and more — are often mislabeled, and state and federal regulations lag far behind.

A 2026 survey estimated that about 5 million Americans have used kratom or similar products, and the increased use has sent kratom-related exposures up 1,200 percent from only 258 exposures in 2015, according to the National Poison Data System.

Sources indicate that now, newer versions of the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms like nausea and vomiting, which are often so severe they bring people to the hospital. Here’s what to know.

Sources indicate that kratom comes from the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Dutch scientist Pieter Willem Korthals first described it in 1839. But “without a doubt, it was used likely for centuries prior to that” in countries including Thailand, Indonesia and Myanmar, indicates Oliver Grundmann, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida in Gainesville. “Wherever there is a stream, these trees are growing there.” People chewed the leaves for a stimulant effect and brewed them into a tea to treat pain,” Grundmann says.

In a recent development, in the United States, kratom is billed pain treatment that is more “natural” than opiates like morphine, Sethi notes. “When you take this product at low doses, it is used for waking up … but at higher doses it becomes opiate-like.” Others take it to treat withdrawal or cravings from opioid use.

The leaf form contains more than 40 different naturally occurring chemicals called alkaloids that could have psychoactive effects. The most key is mitragynine, which makes up two-thirds of the plant’s alkaloid content.

Mitragynine acts on the body’s mu opioid receptors. These receptors — found in the brain, spinal cord and gut — usually respond to natural peptide signals in the body such as endorphins, signaling cells to produce pain relief and release chemicals like dopamine. The receptors get their name from the most famous drug that binds to them: opium. Mitragynine is not derived from or related to opium or morphine but it binds partially to the receptor.

“It’s kind of like a dimmer switch versus turning on the lights,” states Mallory Pullman, a clinical toxicologist at the Mississippi Poison Control Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson. “You don’t fully light your room.”.

Sources indicate that mitragynine also hits receptors that bind norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine receptors, says Grundmann. The activity at adrenergic receptors creates a stimulant-like effect. “Now I think when we look at mitragynine, it’s primarily kind of this duality of the adrenergic and the opioid receptor activity,” he says, producing stimulating and depressive results in turn.

What nature made, chemists and users are happy to tweak.

As the kratom leaf is dried, Grundmann notes, tiny amounts of mitragynine metabolize into another alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. After someone takes kratom, the body also converts some mitragynine to 7-OH. The small chemical tweak changes the compound from one that binds partially to the mu opioid receptors to one that binds fully — like morphine or opium, Grundmann says. 7-OH binds 10 times more strongly to mu opioid receptors than mitragynine does. The resulting product is far more potent in its effects and addictive potential.

When people use the leaves alone, the amount of 7-OH is extremely limited. But by the mid-2010s, scientists found products with more than 500 percent more 7-OH than in the plant alone, and now, consumers can buy products labeled as pure 7-OH.

While 7-OH can be described as “natural” because it can, in theory, occur in nature, toxicologists like Pullman are also seeing synthetic derivatives that are even stronger, including one molecule named MGM-15. MGM-15 is sold as a “research chemical” and is four times more powerful than 7-OH.

What is in kratom products may not always be what’s on the label, leaving owners in the dark about what they are taking. In a 2026 analysis of 44 different kratom products, including tablets, dissolvable films and edibles, Pullman and her colleagues found that 85 percent of the products had contents that did not match the label. Some advertised kratom but contained very high levels of 7-OH. Others had alkaloids that weren’t listed at all.

It’s “very concerning at a consumer level if you can’t trust what’s actually on the label,” Pullman states.

It has been revealed that sethi started hearing the word kratom about 10 years ago in her work with people seeking treatment for opioid use. “I would have patients intermittently tell me about kratom use,” she says. People were using kratom to stay off opioids, or to treat pain, and didn’t report being addicted to the plant.

Now, it’s a different story, Sethi says.

Patients who started using kratom or 7-OH to get off opioids “now are having really bad withdrawal and cravings and ending up in the hospital,” she claims. Some are seeking addiction treatment, not for opioids, but for kratom and 7-OH. In 2025, U.S. poison centers documented 3,434 kratom-related exposure reports, reported both by people who called the center and medical professionals. “I see less fentanyl and more kratom at this point, or more 7-OH,” Sethi says.

According to recent reports, in July of 2026, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily classified some kratom derivatives as Schedule I drugs, meaning they have high abuse potential and no medical use. Those derivatives include 7-OH and another related kratom derivative, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl or MGPI, as well as MGM-15 and its powerful sibling MGM-16. The DEA re-upped the temporary scheduling of MGM-15 and 16 and MGPI in October. 7-OH was temporarily placed in Schedule I at any dose higher than that found in the kratom plant. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has also issued statements warning consumers not to use the products. None of these measures affect the legality of the kratom leaf itself.

Regulations vary at the state level: Twenty-six states don’t regulate kratom at all, while six states and the District of Columbia list kratom’s ingredients as a Schedule I controlled substance, like the current federal scheduling. A further 18 states regulate sale and manufacture in some way.

Recent findings suggest that “I think there’s a lot more concern now, especially that there might be potential opioids out on the market,” Pullman claims. Regulations are trying to thread the needle between banning the plant and banning high-potency derivatives, knowing that when one derivative gets smacked down, another will promptly appear in its place. That cycle is a familiar one, mirroring the evolution and development of synthetic opioids.

In a recent development, “There’s risk with everything,” she notes. “I think it’s notable to distinguish the difference between a synthetic product versus the natural, and that way we can clearly attribute where the risk lies.”.

#7137. Industry News: Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV Review: One Small Step for OLED, One Significant Step for Roku TVs

Industry News: Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV Review: One Small Step for OLED, One Significant Step for Roku TVs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It seems that the rumors of the end of OLED supremacy in the TV marketplace were greatly exaggerated.
  • As you’d expect from Roku, both the baseline Roku Pro Series and the brighter and slightly fancier Roku Pro Series LX are value-oriented models, with list prices that undercut brands like Samsung and LG.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It seems that the rumors of the end of OLED supremacy in the TV marketplace were greatly exaggerated. At the start of 2026, flashy new display technologies like RGB LED emerged to challenge that status quo, theoretically offering a brighter alternative to OLED panels, with greater color coverage. But at the end of the year, OLED TVs, with their ability to control each of a TV’s millions of tiny pixels point-by-point, remain the best option for overall picture performance. In fact, despite the fact that only two companies, LG and Samsung, currently make OLED panels, the number of TV brands that actually use those panels is expanding: Roku, the latest brand to jump into the space, released its first two OLED TVs this fall.

As you’d expect from Roku, both the baseline Roku Pro Series and the brighter and slightly fancier Roku Pro Series LX are value-oriented models, with list prices that undercut brands like Samsung and LG. But like many of our favorite picks at Popular Mechanics, they are designed to balance premium performance and great usability, with a simple setup and handy quality-of-life features that competitors lack, like a built-in remote finder.

After spending several days with the flagship Pro LX, I’m happy to report that Roku’s first foray into OLED TVs is already a strong contender for anyone curious about the benefits of upgrading to an OLED screen. The Pro LX’s picture quality doesn’t quite reach the heights of legacy OLED sets like LG’s C6 let alone flagships like the Samsung’s S95H. But it holds its own, and arguably outdoes them both when it comes to actually living with your TV. If you’re after a best-of-both-worlds OLED approach, the Roku Pro LX is an enticing new option at a very nice price.

Sources indicate that everything about setting up the Pro LX is built around simplicity. Like last year’s LED-powered Roku Pro, the LX eschews multi-piece pedestal stands and tiny bags of screws for feet that attach with screw-on knobs—no tools required. Dual stand positions include higher clearance for a soundbar, though the feet’s width of just over 42 inches on the 65-inch model I tested doesn’t leave much space up front on most consoles. The design doesn’t look quite as stylish as its LG and Samsung rivals, but the build feels stout, and the ultra-thin panel of just over an eighth of an inch up top adds a premium vibe.

Recent findings suggest that the TV turns on automatically when plugged in, and immediately walks you through pairing the voice remote, which charges via USB-C so you never have to worry about batteries. It’s not quite as handy as Samsung’s solar-powered remotes, but its design is intuitive, including options like backlit keys and hands-free “Hey, Roku” voice control. If you’re not into an always-ready mic, you can mute it with a hard switch on the remote’s left edge.

Even the LX’s packaging is designed with forethought, including a plastic screen cover that peels off with a feather-light tug. But before you remove it, you’ll see a yellow arrow that points to my favorite feature by far: A remote finder button. A quick press emits a pleasant chirp from the remote buried in your couch cushions or, if you’ve got a toddler like me, hidden in any number of places out of reach from grabby little hands. I have no idea why this isn’t a standard option across brands, but kudos to Roku. It’s the simple things.

At the TV’s left flank, you’ll find a reasonably well-stocked input hub, including dual HDMI 2.1 inputs for gaming in VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz, an HDMI 2.0 port, and a separate HDMI eARC port for connecting a soundbar or audio system. That’s important because the Pro LX’s sound is particularly thin and weak, all but requiring an audio upgrade. Other inputs in the stack include Ethernet to back up WiFi 6 support, USB-C and USB-A inputs, optical input, and a cable/antenna tuner. It would have been nice to get a full set of four HDMI 2.1 inputs, which you’ll find in similar LG and Samsung TVs, but I appreciate that Roku offers two ways for serious gamers to connect apart from the HDMI eARC port.

Notable features include ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) for fast-paced gaming and support for all major HDR formats, including the top two advanced options, Dolby Vision and HDR10+. In contrast, LG TVs stop at Dolby Vision, while Samsung only offers HDR10+. It’s always nice to have options, and the addition of Dolby Vision, the most common format for streaming, gives Roku a leg-up over Samsung OLEDs.

In a recent development, as you’d expect from an OLED, the Pro LX delivers fantastic contrast between the lightest and darkest images from the moment you turn it on, starting with perfect black levels from its obsidian screen. A polarizing layer does a fine job diffusing reflections for moderately bright rooms, about on par with LG’s C6. It doesn’t offer the powerful ambient light control of matte screens like Samsung’s S90H, but I generally prefer the richer perceived black levels of glossy screens, and the Pro LX is happy to indulge with impressive depth in darker moments.

Roku claims that the Pro LX is around twice as bright as the standard Roku Pro OLED, and after tinkering with the settings a bit, you’ll get plenty of pep to contrast those rich black levels. Using the TV’s most accurate HDR Dark picture mode, I measured around 1200 nits of peak brightness in a 10 percent window with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software.

That’s around 150 nits less than I got with the C6, but the difference is negligible in real-world watching: both TVs look similarly bright in moments like the sun glancing off a windshield or a glowing candle in a dark room. Roku’s model provides more than enough power for impactful HDR punch and vibrant colors, especially since most streaming content tops out at 1,000 nits. Interestingly, you’ll need to change the TV’s separate Picture Brightness setting to the highest “Brighter” mode to unlock that peak brightness. Unfortunately, the picture doesn’t do as good a job following the intent of directors and mastering engineers here as in the dimmer “normal” mode. That noted, while slightly overbright, the TV still looks quite good overall in “brighter” mode. It’s just more of a tradeoff than you’ll see with the C6 at peak brightness.

Recent findings suggest that likewise, the colors aren’t quite as accurate as the C6. You can see the difference in certain specific shades, like the deep oranges in Mad Max: Fury Road, which sometimes looked a little too, well, orangey. I also noticed some color banding, or image artifacts, in especially challenging test scenes, but it rarely showed up in regular films and TV shows.

Recent findings suggest that for most of my viewing, colors looked rich and natural. The vivid coral adventures in Netflix’s Our Planet provide a dazzling rainbow of shades that gave me chills, and watching Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a cinematic experience, with an almost marbled touch to details. There’s enough vibrancy to get you lost in little moments like the flashing gold of Ego’s palace in Guardians of the Galaxy Volume II, or the glowing beads of light reflecting off the Mandalorian’s helmet in his spaceship.

Speaking of space, the TV’s pinpoint light control makes deep-space scenes look incredibly realistic and engaging, especially compared with backlit models like last year’s mini-LED Roku Pro. Shadow details are also impressive, even in challenging scenes from murky highlights like The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, pairing with the TV’s flashy highlights for a lush experience. And while viewing the screen off-angle adds a slight green tinge, as it does with a lot of LG OLEDs, it’s worlds better than the pale colors and accentuated blooming you’ll see in the vast majority of LED TVs. Such is the advantage of OLED.

Of course, the biggest advantage of a Roku-branded OLED is marrying OLED’s technical prowess with a more accessible smart TV operating system. While Sony’s Google TV OLEDs are a solid alternative, Roku OS is notably simpler, more reliable, and in some ways more joyful to use than Samsung’s Tizen, LG’s webOS, and (especially) Panasonic’s Fire TV.

In a recent development, the fact that Roku OS just works exactly the way it’s supposed to is frankly half the battle. I’ve had fewer glitches with Roku OS in several years of TV reviewing than any other system, going back to TCL’s early Roku TVs. On top of that, I like the little extras Roku still offers like space themes, Star Trek-branded wallpaper, and silly movie references in the ever-expanding Roku City screen saver, like Cameron’s dad’s ill-fated Ferrari from Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.

According to recent reports, like all smart TVs I test, Roku OS has gotten less intuitive and more insidious in recent years, from plays to sell your data like ACR (Automatic Content Recognition) to pushier ads, such as a Home Depot-sponsored holiday wallpaper that suddenly appeared as I was writing this review. Luckily, you can turn that and most other annoying features off (though Roku immediately put the ad elsewhere). I’m also not as pleased with the latest Home screen layout, which pushes features like Continue Watching and the full list of apps below (you guessed it) more ads.

The upshot is that it takes more work to reorganize the layout for the best experience, but the good news is you can customize most options, and Roku OS is still the best built-in streaming system I’ve tested.

In a recent development, roku’s Pro Series LX isn’t the best-performing OLED in its class, with both the Samsung S90H and LG C6 providing a cleaner, more accurate picture, but it is comparable and cheaper than either one at full price. (And will likely remain so for the rest of the year as holiday sales kick in.) Moreover, its slick blend of usability and performance could make it the top choice for OLED-curious folks who value a TV’s livability as highly as its picture quality. If you want to make the jump to OLED, and your budget is already stretched, Roku’s your newly introduced go-to.

Other OLED TVs Worth Considering.

#7136. Latest Update: What satellites leave behind
